Use the Data Connect Integration Designer to create integrations

Integration Designer overview

The Integration Designer provides the ability to define data workflows in a low code way.

Note: Consistent with Ellucian's policy for developer documentation, these Integration Designer procedures are provided only in English. Users who select Español as their language on this site will see this Integration Designer documentation in English, and the rest of the Data Connect documentation in Spanish.
These workflows can:
  • Connect to disparate data sources and data formats through Ellucian Ethos.
  • Create data transformations and mappings to third-party sources and formats.
  • Build and maintain integrations through Ethos to third parties.
  • Surface third-party data in Ethos.
Benefits of developing pipelines include:
  • Low-code user interface (UI) for creating integrations.
  • Preview and validation of integrations before sharing with business users.
  • Comprehensive Integration Packages UI that operational users can manage.
  • SaaS safe integrations without an integration server.
  • Ethos native with out-of-the-box support to GET data, POST data, consume change notifications, and run GraphQL queries.
  • Out-of-the-box fittings to parse JSON, XML, and CSV or TSV sources.
  • Support for REST and SOAP calls.
  • Out-of-the-box no-code transformations like Field Mapping, Delimited Formatter or Parser, JSON Formatter or Parser, XML Formatter or Parser, Fixed Width Formatter or Parser, and SFTP Fitting.
  • Configuration-friendly integrations that operational users can customize.
  • Integration packages and pipelines that can be shared across tenants.

Low Code

A low code platform lets you create integrations through visual tools.

For example, you can drag and drop segments, and configure them through context-appropriate dialogs.

As such a platform, the Designer provides a powerful UI to create well-defined integration solutions called pipelines.

Advantages of this approach include:
  • Easy to learn: Available pipeline fittings are simple but highly configurable.
  • Configuration instead of coding: Each pipeline segment provides context-sensitive dialogs, with appropriate help tooltips.
  • Ease of development: Preview and validate integrations, then publish to your business users.
  • Thought for developer personas: Powerful JavaScript fittings for low-level transformations.
  • Portable integration packages: Share packages with clients with the push of a button.

Designer UI overview

Create a new package to group together pipelines with the same objective, or choose one of the existing packages to work with pipelines. When a package has been created, the browser displays the pipeline list screen.

In the top-left corner, inside the packages sidebar, use the + button to create a new package to group together pipelines with the same objective, or choose one of the existing packages to work with pipelines. When a package has been created, the browser displays the pipeline list page.

Pipeline list page

When you click on the following buttons or icons, the corresponding actions occur:

Button or Icon Action
Pipeline and Transform Function tabs Jump between editing pipelines and generic transform functions. Transform functions can be general functions that multiple pipelines can leverage.
Draft and Published filters Available filters display only published pipelines, or only pipelines with a Draft status (pipelines with unpublished changes).
Pipeline Name Navigates to the pipeline designer screen.
Add Pipeline Creates a new pipeline in this package. When a name is specified, it navigates to the pipeline designer screen.
Trash icon Deletes the whole package or pipeline. Requires a confirmation.

Designer page

Button, Icon or Section Description
Return icon < When clicked, returns to the Pipeline List Screen. If there are unsaved changes in the pipeline, a confirmation message appears.
More icon v When clicked, a menu with Pipeline Actions displays. See Pipeline Actions.
Warning icon ! When clicked, shows the fittings that contain missing configuration only when there are.
Action buttons See Action buttons.
Fittings sidebar Shows all available fittings. Hovering over a fitting displays the fitting information. Clicking a fitting adds it to the canvas.
Designer Canvas Shows all the fittings that compose the pipeline. See Fitting Actions.
Right Panel Configuration Right panel either shows the Fitting Configuration when a fitting is selected from the Canvas, or it shows the Pipeline Settings when the Edit Pipeline Settings option is selected from the More menu.

Fitting Actions

When you click the More icon for the fitting, a menu displays with the following actions:

Action Description
Edit Configuration Opens the fitting configuration section on the right panel.
Disable Fitting Disables the fitting.
Move Up Moves the fitting position up in the pipeline.
Move Down Moves the fitting position down in the pipeline.
Delete Fitting Deletes the fitting.

Pipeline Actions

When you click the More Icon v in the top-center of the page, a drop-down menu displays with the following actions:

Action Description
Edit Pipeline Settings Opens the pipeline settings section to add or edit pipeline parameters and enable or disable max concurrency.
Edit Pipeline Name and Description Opens a dialog to edit pipeline name and description.
Delete Pipeline Opens a dialog to delete the pipeline.
Import Pipeline Imports a pipeline from a JSON file.
Export Pipeline Exports a pipeline as a JSON file.

Action buttons

At the top-right corner, you can see the following buttons:

Button Description
Test Tests your current pipeline. You can specify an initial JSON payload if needed, and provide values for parameters. This option is disabled if any fitting is missing the required configuration elements.
Save Saves the current work.
Publish Publishes the current pipeline. You can run and schedule a published pipeline. Specify the version to be published. When published, a pipeline cannot be modified.
Create Draft Creates a draft from a published pipeline. Then, you can use the draft to create the next pipeline version.

First Integration Pipeline: Hello World

You can create an easy-to-follow first pipeline from start to finish.

Before you begin

The user must have Develop permission.

Procedure

Below is a sample payload in JSON format of a call to the persons API:

[
  {"name":"Viktor", "lastName":"Frankestein", "age": 30 },
  {"name":"Agatha","lastName":"De Lacey", "age": 20 },
  {"name":"Elizabeth","lastName":"Lavenza", "age": 22 },
  {"name":"Henry","lastName":"Clerval", "age": 29 },
  {"name":"Creature","age": 2 }
]
Given this input, you can:
  • Transform it into a CSV file with headers.
  • Extrapolate data, such as counting the number of records received and the average age.
  • Redact some sensitive data, such as the age of the persons.
  • Enable downloadable output.
  1. From the Experience dashboard, use either of these methods to access the Integration Designer page:
    • From the Application menu:
      1. Click the Applications icon in the Experience navigation area and then click Integration Designer.
      2. On the Packages page, in the left pane, click the + button to create a new integration package.
    • From the Integration Designer card (if supported at your institution):
      1. Click the Integration Designer card.
      2. On the Packages page, in the left pane, click the + button to create a new integration package.

        A package can have any number of related pipelines. The pop-up requires a package name. A package description is optional.

  2. Select your newly-created package and click +PIPELINE to add a pipeline.
  3. Add a pipeline name.
    A pipeline description is optional.
  4. Click Save.
    The Pipeline Designer displays. A list of available fittings display on the left side of the page. A fitting is a pipeline step. A pipeline contains many of these steps, which are executed in the order they are added.
  5. Expand the Transformations fitting category and select the fitting named Delimited Formatter.
    After you click it, the step is added to the pipeline and that step uses the selected fitting. A warning icon ! next to the TEST button indicates the fitting is not configured yet.
  6. Click the fitting to open the configuration section on the right side of the page.

    You can change the name to be more descriptive, such as Convert to CSV, and add an appropriate description if you want.

    Click the question mark tooltip at the right of each configuration field to learn more about its functionality.

  7. The Delimited Formatter fitting takes a JSON payload and can use a simple JSON path to extract data from said payload. Scroll all the way to the Detail section in the configuration dialog.
  8. Enable the Column Headers so that your output includes the name of the columns. Enter name to specify the path to get the name, and enter Person's Name as the label.
    The fitting evaluates the input like this, and extracts the value for name: {"name":"Agatha","lastName":"De Lacey", "age": 20 }
  9. Even though the pipeline build is not complete, you can run a test at this point. Click TEST at the top of the page.
    The test displays a form where you can execute the pipeline. Most of the pipelines retrieve their initial data from REST endpoints, files, or other data sources; however, you can pass initial data by enabling the Enter JSON Input Data option.
  10. Enable Enter JSON Input Data.
  11. Copy and paste the sample payload at the beginning of this page.
  12. Click RUN TEST.
    Note: This does not apply in this example; however, when testing, be advised that the pipeline may only execute for 60 seconds. Limit your data to a small number of records using filters or other parameters so that the pipeline can complete.
    A Results section displays below your JSON input data. By default the Raw tab result displays, but you might find the Payloads tab easier to read.
  13. Click the Payloads tab to see data formatted as CSV, such as the following: 
    [
  "Person's Name",
  "Viktor",
  "Agatha",
  "Elizabeth",
  "Henry",
  "Creature"
]
  14. Click CANCEL to go back to the configuration view.
  15. Add two more columns by clicking on ADD COLUMN button twice and fill the fields with the next information:

    Column1 - (Path: "lastName", Label: "Last Name") Column2 - (Path: "age", Label: "Age") And the test result, for reference:

    [
  "Person's Name,Last Name,Age",
  "Viktor,,30",
  "Agatha,,20",
  "Elizabeth,,22",
  "Henry,,29",
  "Creature,,2"
]

    You now have a working transformation from JSON to CSV.

  16. On the Configuration page, scroll to the Accumulators section and click ADD ACCUMULATOR.
    Accumulators are custom properties that store values to be used in the footer row. You can input a descriptive name (in this case use ageAvg) and then select the operation you want to execute (in this case Average) for parameter age.
  17. Add a footer to see the accumulated result by scrolling down to the footer section, and clicking on ADD FOOTER.
  18. You need to add a footer that is a literal type. This footer can have interpolation values. Use mustache.js to interpolate values.
    You can use this example in the Value field: Average Age:{{accumulators.ageAvg}}
  19. Run a test to validate that the data now includes a footer row with the average age. 
    [
  "Person's Name,Last Name,Age",
  "Viktor,,30",
  "Agatha,,20",
  "Elizabeth,,22",
  "Henry,,29",
  "Creature,,2",
  "Average Age:20.6"
]

    You must redact age, as it is sensitive data.

  20. Scroll to the Redaction Rules section below Accumulators.
    Similar to Columns, redact can use a JSON path to analyze data from the incoming message.
  21. Redact the age.
    1. Select the type Path to indicate that you will provide the path in the JSON.
    2. Add age to the list by typing it in the Enter Columns field and clicking the + button.
    3. To show that you have the age but are masking it, use "***" as the mask.
    The result below shows the age redacted with the specified mask.
    [
  "Person's Name,Last Name,Age",
  "Viktor,,***",
  "Agatha,,***",
  "Elizabeth,,***",
  "Henry,,***",
  "Creature,,***",
  "Average Age:"
]

    Your first pipeline is complete.

  22. Save your work for use during the exercises.

Before you start

Formalize the elements of the integration strategy before creating a pipeline.

Prerequisites

Requirement Type
Confirm stakeholders have a clear understanding of both the personas and data flow. Business or Strategy
Ensure the APIs that you will use provide you with the correct information. Business or Strategy
Review the available Transformations to help estimate the amount of work.
  • What type of transformations are required?
  • Do the current transformations fulfill the requirements or are additional manual transformations required?
 Design
Determine if crosswalks are needed. Crosswalks are dictionaries that can be referenced inside the pipelines, allowing you to detach data mappings from the pipeline, and allowing each client to setup their own mappings. Strategy or Design
Register your application in Ethos Integration when using Ethos APIs. You need the provided API key to call these endpoints. Technical
Verify endpoints access, including security permissions, etc. is setup. A pipeline requires access to the appropriate data sources, for example from the files stored in an S3 bucket, to SFTP and REST calls, to APIs being correctly set up. Technical

Useful info

Pipelines can use Ethos APIs as data sources or as destinations, requiring only a valid API key. Review the OpenAPI documentation for the APIs your pipelines will use to become familiar with the data types, versions, and RESTful actions available.

You can find the available APIs in the API Catalog. The OpenAPI documentation is available for each API through the catalog.

Data Connect pipeline types

Integration pipelines

Integration pipelines should be used for long running and scheduled batch jobs.

They should also be used when integrating external data and applying transforms in Insights. They can also be used to generate and download files from the UI.

Diagnostic logs

A diagnostic log file can be generated when testing an integration pipeline.

See Troubleshooting: Enable diagnostic logs for more details.

Concurrency

Integration pipelines use concurrency, also known as multithreading or parallelism, when a forEach section is encountered on the pipeline. At that moment, pipelines are automatically divided into one or more phases. Each phase consists of one or more segments, and some phases can be parallel. When a phase runs in parallel, it divides up the work into multiple jobs, one for each message that needs to be processed, to speed up processing time.

After all the records are processed, the engine will fan-in the results into an array and push each message of the aggregated results to the next phase.

Note: Consider that multiple partial jobs can be reading or posting data to the APIs at the same time, and that might cause additional load on the client APIs.

To see the parallel execution plan for your pipeline, you can enable the Diagnostic Log when the pipeline is executed as a job. The zip file will include a plan.json file, indicating which phases will run in parallel (the runInParallel attribute).

Max job concurrency can be tuned through the Job page. The default value for concurrency is 10, which means that a maximum of 10 jobs can be consuming APIs at the same time. This value can be turned up or down to tune the performance, from 1 to 50. Greater concurrency will mean a faster processing speed, but a higher load on the target APIs.

In addition, the default maximum concurrency value can be changed from the Designer. It is still tied to the 1 to 50 range, but this will limit the maximum concurrency value that you can set on a Job screen. The new default maximum value can be set by clicking the drop-down menu aside the pipeline name and then selecting Edit Pipeline Settings in the Designer, selecting the Max Concurrency tab and then turning the Set Max Concurrency switch on. Doing this allows you to adjust the value, just like on the Job Screen.

This setting will limit the value on the Job creation screen. Consequently, operational users will be able to set a max concurrency value in the New Job or Edit Job screen to anything less than or equal to the max concurrency value set in the Designer.

Note: One key difference between testing in the designer and running an integration pipeline as a job, is that parallelism is activated for jobs. Designer test runs are not parallelized.

See Common patterns for more details about concurrency.

Data Connect Serverless APIs

Serverless APIs are pipelines meant to be short-running and cannot run for longer than 60 seconds.

Serverless APIs can be called from a custom Experience card without deploying an intermediate authorization proxy. Serverless APIs can also be called by a 3rd party through Ethos Integration to fulfill custom JSON data requests.

Serverless APIs do not support multiple concurrent threads for processing.

For information on how to develop Integration Designer serverless APIs, see Develop serverless APIs.

Develop pipelines

Several concepts apply to both Integration Pipelines and Serverless APIs.

Packages

A package, also known as an integration package, logically groups one or more pipelines. The package can also include other artifacts, such as transform functions. The Designer provides a seamless workflow to create and maintain integration packages.

While only a name is required, having a brief package description helps identify its purpose. Ellucian recommends that all pipelines contained in a package share a common use-case scenario.

Pipelines

A pipeline is a collection of sequential steps called segments. By properly organizing and configuring each segment, a myriad of simple and complex tasks are achievable. Each segment in a pipeline is an instance of a fitting precisely configured to perform a specific task.

Like packages, pipelines are internally managed as versioned JSON documents. The pipeline Designer provides a simple drag-and-drop user interface to effectively build pipelines without any of the JSON configuration complexities.

This is an example of a pipeline created with the Designer and exported:

{
  "name": "extractDataFromServerA",
  "pipeline": [
    "getApplicants",
    "forEachApplicant",
    "getApplicantChoices",
    "mergeChoicesWithApplicant"
  ],
  "segments": {
    "getApplicants": {
      "class": "ethosProxyGet",
      "config": { "resource": "applicants", "acceptVersions": ["1"] }
    },
    "forEachApplicant": {
      "class": "forEach"
    },
    "getApplicantChoices": {
      "class": "ethosProxyGetFilter",
      "config": {
        "resource": "applicant-choices",
        "acceptVersions": ["1"],
        "filter": "?applicant={{applicant.id}}"
      }
    },
    "mergeChoicesWithApplicant": {
      "class": "JavaScriptTransform",
      "config": { "artifactName": "mergeData" }
    }
  }
}

Fittings and segments

The relationship between fittings and segments is tightly coupled.

A pipeline contains a set of segments and each defines and configures fitting execution. You must execute fittings and segments at the same time. It is important to know the differences between fittings and segments.

Fittings

Fittings are basic building blocks capable of performing functions. They are configured with segments.

Each fitting has a very specific purpose. Fittings are classified into three main types:
  • Sources - enable the pipeline to fetch data from internal and external resources.
  • Transformations - allow you to change or act upon data.
  • Destinations - enable the pipeline to send data to internal and external resources.

Most fittings provide a configuration setting to fine-tune their execution logic, making them highly customizable and versatile. Their execution logic gets triggered as soon as a message is received. And while many fittings will produce another message in return, that is not the case with some Destination types.

Among many other things, you can use these fittings to:
  • Consume Ethos resources
  • Parse and format JSON, XML, fixed-width, and delimited files
  • Request generic HTTP resources
  • Transform data

A list of currently supported fittings can be found in the Available fittings documentation.

Segments

Segments are instances of fittings configured to perform a specific task. Every segment has three base configuration settings: Name, Description, and Execution condition.

Field Description Required
Name Segment name. The Designer will automatically set it to the fitting name. You can change this to something more appropriate with no negative consequences. Yes
Description Self-documenting field that describes the purpose of the segment. No
Execution Condition

Provides a way to conditionally execute the segment based on a defined reference from a context field, message header, or message payload.

For example, a boolean pipeline parameter can be used (context.someFlag), or a boolean variable in the message payload, such as from a JavaScript transform (message.payload.someFlag).

Evaluated at run-time, the resulting value must be of type boolean (true or false). When true the segment will be executed, otherwise it will be skipped.

You can use multiple conditions by combining them logically, using commas to separate them, with no spaces between conditions. For example, use:

message.payload.condition1,context.condition2

All conditions must evaluate to true for the segment to execute.

 No

Some fittings will provide additional configuration fields in addition to name, description, and execution condition. See Available fittings documentation for explanations of additional configurations.

Multiple execution conditions

Example:

{
  "name": "chained conditions",
  "pipeline": [
    "JavaScript Transform",
    "Add To Context",
    "JavaScript Transform1"
  ],
  "segments": {
    "JavaScript Transform": {
      "class": "JavaScriptTransform",
      "config": {
        "pushUndefined": true,
        "stopOnError": false,
        "code": "function transform (message, context) {\n  message.payload.condition1=true\n  message.payload.toContext=true\n  return message;\n}\n"
      }
    },
    "Add To Context": {
      "class": "addToContext",
      "config": {
        "source": "toContext",
        "target": "condition2"
      }
    },
    "JavaScript Transform1": {
      "class": "JavaScriptTransform",
      "if": "message.payload.condition1,context.condition2",
      "config": {
        "pushUndefined": true,
        "stopOnError": false,
        "code": "function transform (message, context) {\n  message.payload ={}\n  message.payload.text='Execution conditon executed correctly!'\n  return message;\n}\n"
      }
    }
  }
}

Messages

Data moves through a pipeline using messages. A message is an envelope composed of two main parts: a header and a payload.

The header is an object structure designed to contain metadata, and is mainly used for informational purposes. Some fittings will automatically add header fields to report certain execution aspects. These headers are useful when debugging a pipeline. The header can also be leveraged as a vehicle for auxiliary data storage by using the JavascriptTransform fitting. However, header persistence is not guaranteed. Some fittings will pluck the header out of the message, or even reset it, making it a volatile aspect of a message.

Note: Avoid deleting, setting to null, or setting to undefined the message.header or message.payload in JavaScript Transform steps, as this can lead to inconsistent behavior at runtime.

The payload, on the other hand, is the container that transports the data being processed and transformed by the pipeline. A payload can contain data of the following types:

Type Description Example
string Plain and simple text value. "Hello, my name is John."
array List of values. Each value in the list can be of type string, number, boolean (true or false flags), object, or another array. ["Foo", "Bar", "Baz"]
object Complex structure consisting of key and value pairs where key is the name of a property, and the value can be of type string, number, boolean (true or false flags), array, or another object. { first: "John", last: "Smith", age: 43, married: true }
buffer Used to represent a continuous sequence of text characters, mainly used when streaming data from one segment to another. N/A

The payload content can (and will) change as data moves from one segment to the other. It is also important to be aware of what type of payload a fitting expects, and what type of payload it will return. For instance, the DelimitedFormatter fitting accepts string payloads, and produces object payloads. This input or output criteria is very important when connecting one segment with another.

There are some exceptional fittings that do not use messages to transport data. See Available fittings documentation.

Pipeline parameters and context

Even though messages are used to transport data from one segment to another, they are dynamic by nature — their values will inevitably change as the pipeline progresses. Use message data references on a segment configuration only when it is certain data will exist within the header or payload.

Pipeline parameters and the context can be used for a more consistent source of information across all segments.

Parameters

Parameters are values that the user can define before pipeline execution.

For example, consider a pipeline built to extract and process data for students of a certain year. The year can be hard-coded right into the pipeline configuration, but it would make for a very rigid one, limited to that specific year. Instead, you can define a parameter to hold the year and use it within the logic of the pipeline. Then, the pipeline is flexible enough to use for any year.

Parameters are optional: a pipeline can declare one or more, or no parameters at all.

The pipeline Designer provides an easy way to add new parameters. Clicking the drop-down menu next to the pipeline name and then selecting Edit Pipeline Settings opens the Pipeline Settings panel. With the Pipeline Parameters tab selected, you can update or delete existing parameters; and, you can add new parameters by clicking the + PARAMETER button.

The only required field for a parameter declaration is its Name, but a wide array of options are available for a deeper parameter customization:

Field Description Example
Persistent parameter

When you select this check box, this parameter persists across all jobs. You can assign it with the "Setup" permission.

Changing a Required parameter from persistent to non-persistent, or from non-persistent to persistent, will force a major version upgrade.

true
Name

It should be a single word (no spaces). This name will serve as an access key within the context object. It is not permissible to declare reserved parameter names (see note below).

If the user types the keyword ethosApiKey, an alert displays and it is automatically marked as sensitive.

 year
Label User friendly label. It displays on pipeline execution forms. It supports localization. Academic Year
Description Extended parameter description (currently used for documentation purposes). It supports localization. Year used to extract students.
Required Defines if it is necessary to provide the parameter value before executing a pipeline job. true
Sensitive

Defines if it is necessary to obfuscate the parameter value to protect its content. Parameters marked as Sensitive cannot have default values.

 false
Type Data type the parameter will accept. The following types are supported: String, Number, Boolean, Array, Date Time, and File. Some types will reveal additional validation fields. For the File Type, the maximum file size supported is 650 MB. Number
Default Value

Value the parameter will have if the field is left blank on pipeline execution forms. This is not supported on parameters of type File.

Default values are not allowed (blocked) if you are using sensitive parameters.

When testing, values for sensitive parameters are saved in the browser for the duration of the Integration Designer session.

If you test the pipeline, you can use the default value in the memory.

 2021
Enum Short for Enumeration, it contains a list of possible values a parameter can contain. Only available for types String and Number, it provides a restricted value selection experience on pipeline execution forms. N/A

All pipeline execution forms present the operational user with a section where they can enter parameter values. All parameter values transfer to the context after executing the pipeline.

Persistent parameters

To make a parameter available for all jobs after you create or edit it, click the This parameter will be persisted across all jobs. It can be assigned with the "Setup" permission check box.

After a job is created or edited with persistent parameters, you will need to save the pipeline and publish a new version. Because previously-created jobs will still have the sensitive values visible, Ellucian recommends that after you successfully create all of the new jobs, you delete your previous jobs, so that users are not able to go in and view the sensitive values you want hidden, such as the API key. The final user requires Experience Setup permissions to set up the parameter.

The pipeline can then be published. When you publish, the system will force you to update to a new version.

After publishing, you can assign the values on the Integration Packages card, by selecting the pipeline and navigating to the Pipeline parameters tab. To access this page, the user requires the Setup permissions, in addition to either View or Manage permissions for the parent package of the pipeline.

When parameters are also marked as sensitive, after they are saved and the user navigates back to the page, they can no longer see that value. You can only mark String, Number or Array parameters as persistent and sensitive.

Sensitive parameters

When a value is flagged as Sensitive, it is masked in the user interface and in diagnostic logs.

Parameters marked as Sensitive cannot have default values.

The types of values that should have a sensitive flag include API keys, SFTP passwords or private keys, OAuth Client ID, and Secret values for third party OAuth endpoints.

Data Connect changes the parameter as sensitive and shows an alert in the following scenarios when they are not marked as sensitive:
  • A pipeline parameter used in the Private Key or Password field on the SFTP fittings.
  • A pipeline parameter used in the Secret Access Key field on the File fittings.
  • A pipeline parameter used in the API key field on the Ethos fittings.
  • A pipeline parameter used in the OpenAI API Key field on the OpenAI Chat Completions fitting.

About reserved parameter names

The name of reserved parameters starts with double underscore (__). You cannot declare reserved parameters as pipeline parameters.

The following parameters (entries in pipeline context) are automatically populated by the framework:

  • __runId - Unique identifier for the current pipeline execution. Always set.
  • __tenantId - GUID of the tenant for which the pipeline is executing. Always set.
  • __lastRunCreated - The date and time of the last run of the current pipeline was initialized. Not guaranteed to be set.
  • __lastSuccessfulRunCreated - The date and time of the last run of the current pipeline was successfully completed. Not guaranteed to be set.
  • __pipelineName - The name of the pipeline being executed. Always set.
  • __user - User object. Only set when at least one user field is included.
  • id - Set to the Ethos Person ID of the end user, if available.
  • __region - AWS region.
  • __stage - Indicates if is Dev, Test or Prod.
  • __regionTld - This changes depending on the region, Example: .com for usa or .au for Australia.

Legacy parameter names runId, tenantId, lastRunCreated, and lastSuccessfulRunCreated are still supported for backwards compatibility. Ellucian recommends using the double underscore (__) convention to invoke reserved parameters.

Special reserved parameters

The following parameters can be set by the pipeline logic, allowing the modification of a pipeline result.

  • __httpStatusCode (number) - If set, when invoking an API Pipeline, Data Connect uses the value as the HTTP Status code response.
  • __httpStatusMessage (string|object|number) - If set, when invoking an API Pipeline, Data Connect uses the value as the HTTP Status code message.

See: Return custom HTTP status.

Context

The context is a centralized data repository accessible to all segments. As soon as a pipeline job is started, all parameter values are made available through the context. Pipeline creators can also leverage the context; the AddToContext and JavaScriptTransform fittings provide a convenient interface to create segments that extend the context with new fields. When a new field is added to the context, it is automatically accessible to all segments in the pipeline.

The only caveat when using the context is that you cannot update or delete the value of a field after you add it.

Note: Context fields are immutable. This feature is meant to maintain the integrity of input parameters (and other internal fields) across the pipeline execution lifetime.

Be aware that context might not be shared during distributed execution of pipelines. See Integration pipelines for more information.

Crosswalks

Crosswalks are powerful dictionaries you can tailor per tenant, allowing one pipeline to generate different outputs.

For example, "Client A wants to convert code 'ABC' to 'BCD' and client B wants to convert the same code to 'XYZ'," is a perfect fit for crosswalks, as it allows different clients to specify different outputs.

JavaScript transform functions

JavaScript (JS) Transform Functions are a way to handle data in a custom manner, allowing you to interact with messages and the pipeline's context to transform any data into a desired output.

A JavaScriptTransform fitting uses a JS Transform Function with the option to write an inline function in the Designer, which is available only when that fitting is being executed, or referencing an Externalize JavaScript transform functions JS file, which is available through the whole lifecycle of a pipeline. Externalized JS Transform Functions, can be referenced in any amount of pipelines within the same integration package.

The function must be named transform and it must accept at least one parameter, which is the message. It can also accept a second parameter that will hold the pipeline’s context. Values may be obtained from the pipeline context using context.get('key'). You can also use the context.set function to add new values to the context from within a transform; a transform that accepts a key and a value as parameters.

In addition, the JS Transform Function should always end with a return statement. Data Connect pushes the returned value forward to the next pipeline segment. However, returning a message is not strictly required.

If the function throws an exception (or external conditions throw an exception, for example an execution timeout) and a stopOnError flag has been configured inside the JavaScriptTransform fitting to be true, any further messages are dropped, effectively stopping the pipeline.

Here is an example of a JavaScript Transform Function:

function transform (message, context) {
  // Transform logic here
  return message;
}

It is important to note that a JS Transform Function is executed in a sandbox, and may not require or import any modules.

Pipeline execution lifecycle

Whether they are scheduled or ad-hoc, when a pipeline is executed its lifecycle depends entirely on messages flowing between segments. As soon as message emission stops, pipeline execution ends.

Starting

By default, an empty message is automatically fed into the first segment to jump-start the pipeline execution. It is good practice to retrieve (or generate) data at the beginning of the pipeline so that it is processed along the way.

Source fittings are particularly useful to retrieve data from Ethos, SFTP, or the built-in file repository among other sources. These fittings will accept an incoming message, and either extend or replace its data before forwarding a message to the next segment. Other source fittings will stream data through multiple messages, easing the transmission burden of big data loads. Refer to the Available fittings documentation for more details.

Message processing

When a pipeline is in progress, segments sequentially receive and emit messages until all messages have been processed. Even though the pipeline starts with just one message, some fittings are designed to emit one or more messages.

As long as there is a message in transit, each segment in the pipeline sequence gets an opportunity to execute its underlying logic.

Note: The only way to conditionally include (or exclude) a segment from the execution chain is by configuring its Execute Condition. Execute conditions are references that can point to context, message header, or message payload values. When specified, only if the reference evaluates to true the segment will be executed; otherwise, the segment will be skipped and the message forwarded to the next segment in line (if any).

Ending

A pipeline execution ends when one of the following events happen:

  • Last message reaches the end of the pipeline or endpoint segment.
  • Exceptions thrown by JavascriptTransform segments.

It is good practice to save transformed data on or before the end of the pipeline. Destination fittings are particularly useful to send data to Ethos, SFTP, or the built-in file repository among other destinations. Be aware that most destination fittings produce endpoint segments. Refer to the Available fittings documentation for more details.

When the last pipeline segment processes the last message, the execution job naturally reaches its end. Endpoint segments, on the other hand, can create a premature end even when located by mid-pipeline; effectively stopping a message transmission before reaching the last segment.

About endpoint segments

The word endpoint describes a segment that receives and processes a message, but will not emit any messages. Consequently, Data Connect does that execute any following segments. Most destination fittings produce endpoint segments, while some you can configure some to avoid this default behavior.

An exception, in most cases, is an unexpected situation found within the logic of a segment for a given message. These exceptions are reported for future troubleshooting, but the pipeline continues. There is also the possibility of using the JavascriptTransform fitting to configure a segment that can voluntarily raise an exception to completely halt the pipeline execution; any current or pending messages will not be processed.

Available Fittings

See Available fittings documentation for a list of fittings divided by functionality.

Sub-pipelines

When you create an integration pipeline, you can mark it as a sub-pipeline to add an extra step or sub-process to existing pipelines.

You will see an option to select the This is a sub-pipeline check box when you create a pipeline.

After you create and publish a sub-pipeline, it displays as an option to be selected in the Sub-pipeline fitting. The Sub-pipeline fitting is used to select the sub-pipeline to be run at that step in the pipeline. See Sub-pipeline fitting.

There are some things to consider with sub-pipelines:
  • Pipelines marked as sub-pipelines can not be run standalone.
  • You can only invoke sub-pipelines that have been shared to you or that you have published.
  • The sub-pipeline fitting is not available for Serverless API pipelines.
  • Sub-pipelines cannot be nested.
  • Sub-pipelines can not have persistent parameters.
  • A pipeline can have many sub-pipeline fittings.
  • The context of the parent pipeline is passed to the sub-pipeline. There is no need to specify which parameters are sent.
  • You cannot import a pipeline if it has persistent parameters or if it has sub-pipeline fittings in it.
  • Defining input schema is optional, but can be useful.
  • Sub-pipelines are run synchronously. Sub-pipeline steps are merged into the main pipeline steps and run as a single job.
  • You can import a sub-pipeline, as long as the pipeline being imported does not use the Sub-pipeline fitting, and does not have persistent parameters.
  • You can export a sub-pipeline.

Pipeline context execution limit

The total amount of data stored in pipeline context is limited to 2.5 GB per execution. This includes data added using the Add to Context fitting or variables set using context.set() in a JavaScript Transform. Pipelines that exceed this limit fail with a clear error message.

To avoid exceeding the pipeline context limit, follow these best practices:
  • Store only essential data in pipeline context.
  • Avoid accumulating large arrays or full payload copies in context.
  • Use file-based storage (File Writer and File Reader fittings) for large datasets instead of storing them in context.
  • Remove context variables that are no longer needed.
  • Test pipelines using representative data volumes before moving to production.

Developer workflow

A pipeline that has already been developed in the Designer can be published so it becomes available to Integration Packages.

After it is published, a Pipeline can be viewed on the Integration Packages user interface (UI) and jobs can be created for it.

There are two ways to develop a pipeline: You can create a pipeline from scratch using the + PIPELINE button on Integration Designer or you can open an already existing pipeline and click CREATE DRAFT. Both these options create a draft pipeline that can then be edited in the Designer. The second option creates a draft copy of an already published pipeline, which can be modified per your requirements before being published.

The First Integration Pipeline: Hello World provides instructions and a first pipeline example you can use as reference when developing a pipeline.

When development of a pipeline in the designer is completed and the pipeline is tested to ensure that it runs successfully, click the Publish button on the Designer to publish the pipeline. The Publish button is only enabled on the Designer when all fitting configurations on the pipeline are complete. Proceed to the publishing process section to publish a pipeline.

Publish integration pipelines

A pipeline that has already been developed in the Designer can be published so it becomes available to Integration Packages.

About this task

Publishing a pipeline makes it available to clients to create jobs. A job is a pipeline that is scheduled to run, either as soon as possible or in the future. After a job is created and executed at least once, a job run is available to view on the Pipeline Runtime dashboard. If a job is scheduled to run once, it only ever has one job run. If a job is scheduled to run on a recurring basis, it has a job run for every recurrence.

An unpublished pipeline is considered a draft. Draft pipelines are viewed from the Integration Designer. A draft pipeline can be deleted by clicking on the trash icon under the Actions menu. After a pipeline is published, it can only be deleted if is not currently shared.

Clicking on the name of the draft pipeline opens up the pipeline in Designer where you can either edit or publish the pipeline.

Procedure

  1. Click the name of the draft pipeline to open the pipeline in Designer.
  2. If all fitting configurations are complete and if all the fittings are enabled, the PUBLISH button is enabled. If PUBLISH is disabled, check the errors badge at the left of the test button to make sure that a fitting does not have an incomplete configuration or is disabled.
  3. When ready, click on the PUBLISH button. This action displays the Publish Pipeline dialog.
    This dialog asks for confirmation of pipeline publish and recommends a test run to ensure that the pipeline is valid. The recommended release version options are displayed. See: Pipeline versioning guidelines
  4. Select the required version (following the guidelines above) and click PUBLISH.
    On successful publication, the Designer closes and the Integration Designer displays with the updated pipeline status. In case of failure, the dialog closes and you are returned to Designer where an error message displays at the top of the designer.
  5. After your pipeline is successfully published, if it needs to be further edited, create a new draft of the pipeline. To do this, click on the name of the pipeline to enter Designer. The Designer displays the pipeline in "read only" mode. Fittings cannot be added and pipeline configuration cannot be edited.
  6. To create a new draft of this pipeline, click the CREATE DRAFT button.
    This creates a draft version of the pipeline. The pipeline saved successfully message displays and any edits can now be performed on the pipeline. On the Integration Designer the new draft pipeline displays and the draft column displays an info icon. Hover over the icon or tab to it to display the original pipeline from which the draft was created.
    The draft pipeline can be edited, new fittings can be added, or parameters can be edited or added as per your requirements. If any change is made to required parameters or if any new required parameters are added, you need to publish a major version of the pipeline.
  7. After development is completed on the draft, click the PUBLISH button to publish this pipeline. As a new required parameter has been added, the publish pipeline dialog informs you that pipeline version will be updated to the next major version. If no breaking changes are made, the dialog displays with options to choose next patch, minor, or major version.
    When you click PUBLISH, the pipeline publishes with version, as per your selection (or next major version in case of breaking changes) and the newly published pipeline displays in the Integration Designer.
    If you do not make any breaking changes and publish a patch or minor version of the pipeline, then only the latest patch or minor version (of each major version) displays. If, for example, you published 0.0.1, 0.0.2 and 1.0.0 versions, only 0.0.2 and 1.0.0 display because they are the latest versions of 0.x and 1.x major versions respectively.
    The pipeline is now successfully published.
  8. Apply permissions for roles before the pipeline is visible. For an Integration pipeline, permissions for the package need to be given to a role. Then, it will be available in the Integration Packages UI.
  9. Optional: If there is an Integration Pipeline breaking change, the following scenarios require a new major version number:
    Regular parameters
    Case Marked as required Force major Justification
    A parameter name is changed. Yes Yes Any existing Experience page could fail to start the pipeline because the parameter is not registered with a value.
    A parameter name is changed. No No Because the parameter is optional, it should not be considered necessary to execute the pipeline.
    A parameter type is changed. Yes Yes Any existing Experience page could fail to start the pipeline because the parameter is the wrong type.
    A parameter type is changed. No Yes If the pipeline starts failing due to validation then this is considered a breaking change if the parameter was provided, so it requires a major version update.
    A parameter is added. Yes Yes If it has no default value, the pipeline may fail to start.
    A parameter is added. No No Because the parameter is optional, it should not be considered necessary to execute the pipeline.
    A parameter is deleted. Yes Yes When a parameter is removed, it should be considered a breaking change.
    A parameter is deleted. No No Because the parameter is optional, it should not be considered necessary to execute the pipeline.
    A parameter was changed to Required from Optional. Yes Yes Changing a parameter from optional to required means that because it was optional before, it may not have been registered with a value, and therefore the pipeline could fail to start.
    A parameter was changed to Optional from Required. No No When a required parameter changes to optional, it should not be considered a breaking change.
    A required parameter with a default value is changed to a sensitive parameter. Yes Yes When a required parameter changes from normal to sensitive and there is a default value, the default value is removed and needs to be set by the end user.

Pipeline versioning guidelines

There are versioning guidelines for pipelines.

Follow the pipeline versioning the guidelines listed below:

  • Pipelines must be versioned using Semantic Versioning.
  • Pipelines must use a new major version number when a breaking change is made. See Publish integration pipelines for the table that describes breaking changes.
  • A new minor or patch version does not require you to do anything. Existing jobs or Serverless APIs will continue to work.
  • A new major version requires you to set up a new job for the pipeline.

Develop serverless APIs

After you create a serverless API draft, you can optionally define input or output schemas.

Create a serverless API

Follow the step-by-step instructions on how to create a serverless API.

Procedure

  1. From the Experience dashboard, use either of the following methods to access your integration package:
    • From the Application menu:
      1. Click the Applications icon in the Experience navigation area, and then click Integration Packages.
      2. On the Integration Packages page, in the left pane, select the package you want to create the pipeline on.
    • From the Integration Packages card (if supported at your institution):
      1. Click the Integration Designer card.
      2. On the Data Connect integration packages card on the Experience dashboard, select the package you want to create the pipeline on.
  2. Click the + PIPELINE button.
    A dialog box displays with several fields to configure the pipeline.
  3. By default, the Integration Pipeline Type is selected. To create a serverless API, select API from the Pipeline Type drop-down.
  4. Enter a unique name for your pipeline.
    Note: A warning displays if the same name already exists in the system. As the pipeline works as an API resource, the name should not contain spaces.
  5. Choose the appropriate HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) based on the actions you plan to perform in your pipeline.
    Note: GET requests cannot receive a body.
  6. Select the desired authentication type (User token or Ethos token) based on your pipeline's authentication requirements.
    1. Select User token if the pipeline is called from an Experience card.
    2. Select Ethos token if the pipeline is called through the Ethos Integration proxy by an external application.
    3. See Authorization for more details on authorization requirements and setup.
  7. Optional: Provide a description for the pipeline to clarify the purpose or functionality of the pipeline.
  8. Click Save to create a draft of the pipeline within the package.
    You can now proceed with further configurations, such as defining input and output schema and building the pipeline using the fittings and pipeline parameters.

Configure serverless API behavior

After creating the Serverless API draft, optional input or output schemas can be defined.

About this task

Defining schema can ensure an appropriate validation is executed against the received input or generated output. See the section Create schemas for a detailed guide on schemas.

Procedure

  1. Define Pipeline parameters.
    1. For example, parameters for an API key or an Id parameter can be defined.
    2. After it is published, the pipeline will be invocable with an HTTP request. The HTTP request parameters are bound to the pipeline parameters.
  2. Optional: If you expect a certain data input for the pipeline and you would like to validate it, define an input schema.
  3. Add appropriate fittings to fulfill your use case.
    1. For example, add an Ethos Proxy Get to retrieve information from an Ethos resource.
    2. You can use values from the parameters, payload, or context to refine the request.
    See Available fittings documentation for more information.
  4. Configure the output as expected. See About creating a response for details.
    1. The response must be a single message. If the pipeline is configured to return an array, the message should contain an array.
    2. A custom HTTP status can also be defined. See: Return custom HTTP status.
  5. Optional: Define an output schema to validate the output.

Import an existing pipeline

It is possible to import an existing pipeline JSON file into the Designer. However, the pipeline must match the API type. If an attempt is made to import an integration pipeline when working on a serverless API the import will fail.

Test the pipeline draft before publishing

The Test button can be used to test the pipeline logic. However, it will not fully simulate a HTTP API call.

About this task

These are the differences when testing with the Test dialog:
  • Input and output schema validation is not checked.
  • No value will be injected in context._user (See: Obtain the current user ID value)
  • A value should be hard set, as needed for testing.
  • If a custom HTTP code or message were used, the test response will include those overridden values in the result shown in the test window.

Publish and execute a serverless API

After you publish a serverless API, a Platform Component is created in Ethos Integration.

Procedure

  1. Click Publish to publish a pipeline version.

    See: Pipeline versioning guidelines.

    There are scenarios that are considered a breaking change, and therefore require a new major version number. See below for specific scenarios.

    Input schema properties
    Case Marked as required Force major Justification
    A property name is changed. Yes Yes Any existing Experience page could fail to start the pipeline because the property is not registered with a value.
    A property name is changed. No No Because the property is optional, it should not be considered necessary to execute the pipeline.
    A property type is changed. Yes Yes Any existing Experience page could fail to start the pipeline because the property is the wrong type.
    A property type is changed. No Yes If the API starts failing due to validation, then this would be considered a breaking change, so it requires a major version update.
    A property is added. Yes Yes If it has no default value, the pipeline may fail to start.
    A property is added. No No Because the property is optional, it should not be considered necessary to execute the pipeline.
    A property is deleted. Yes Yes When a property is removed, it should be considered a breaking change.
    A property is deleted. No No Because the property is optional, it should not be considered necessary to execute the pipeline.
    A property was changed from optional to required. Yes Yes Changing a property from optional to required means that because it was optional before, it may not have been registered with a value, and therefore the pipeline could fail to start.
    A property was changed from required to optional. No No When a required property changes to optional, it should not be considered a breaking change.
    Output schema properties
    Case Marked as required Force major Justification
    A property name is changed. Yes Yes Any existing Experience page could fail to start the pipeline because the property is not registered with a value.
    A property name is changed. No Yes This would be a breaking change because it may break the contract for the API.
    A property type is changed. Yes Yes Any existing Experience page could fail to start the pipeline because the property is the wrong type.
    A property type is changed. No Yes If the API starts failing due to validation, then this would be considered a breaking change, so it requires a major version update.
    A property is added. Yes Yes If it has no default value, the pipeline may fail to start.
    A property is added. No No Because the property is optional, it should not be considered necessary to execute the pipeline.
    A property is deleted. Yes Yes When a property is removed, it should be considered a breaking change.
    A property is deleted. No Yes This would be a breaking change because it may break the contract for the API.
    A property was changed from optional to required. Yes Yes Changing a property from optional to required means that because it was optional before, it may not have been registered with a value, and therefore the pipeline could fail to start.
    A property was changed from required to optional. No Yes This would be considered a breaking change, because it may break the contract for the API.
    After it is published, a Platform Component is created in Ethos Integration.
  2. To confirm a Platform Component was created, navigate to Ethos Integration and select the Platform Components tab
  3. Select the Data Connect card.
    The published serverless API name displays under the Owned Resources tab.
  4. Confirm the application for which the API key will be used is listed under the Platform Components- Data Connect- Application Access list.
    Before executing the serverless API, appropriate authorization needs to be set up:
    • If the pipeline was configured to require a 'User Token':
      • Permissions are automatically pushed to Experience Permissions.
      • The final user's role will need to be assigned the 'Execute' action for the specific pipeline.
      • See: Authorization for more details.
    • If the pipeline was configured to require an 'Ethos token': An appropriate tag must be added. See: Authorization

    Then, the pipeline can be executed.

Example

The following cUrl will execute a POST to the latest serverless API named 'exampleServerlessAPI':

curl --location 'https://integrate.elluciancloud.com/api/exampleServerlessAPI?year=2023' 
--header 'Content-Type: application/json' --header 'Accept: application/json' --header 'Authorization: Bearer {{validTokenValue}}' --data '{"id": "12345"}'

The following cUrl will execute a GET to the execute version 1.0.3 of a serverless API named 'anotherExample':

curl --location --request GET 'https://integrate.elluciancloud.com/api/anotherExample' --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --header 'Accept: application/vnd.hedtech.integration.v1.0.3+json' --header 'Authorization: Bearer {{validTokenValue}}'

Note that GET requests cannot receive a body.

The examples above can be used as a basis to execute serverless APIs from third party applications. The URL might change depending on the desired execution region.

See Execute serverless APIs from Experience extensions for a guide to executing the serverless API from Experience.

About pipeline versioning

Pipelines are published using semantic versioning.

See Pipeline versioning guidelines.

See API Behaviors.

When executing pipelines, the 'accept' header will indicate which version of the pipeline to execute, or the value 'application/json' can be used to retrieve the latest version of the pipeline.

Using the latest version is recommended during development trials, to ensure an up-to-date pipeline definition is used. For production usage, at least a major version should be specified, as pipeline definitions are cached to speed up the execution process.

At this time, it's not possible to publish 'beta' versions.

About the input message

The payload of the HTTP request, if any, will be passed in the 'payload' property of the initial message.

Examples

A payload in the following form will be wrapped into a Data Connect message:

{"id":12345}

will be wrapped in a Data Connect message and passed as:

{
   header:{}
   payload:{"id":12345}
}

Note: in the Test dialog, the first simple form can be used. If the payload is a valid Data Connect message, it will be passed as is:

{
   "header": { "initial": 1 },
   "payload": { "data": "example data"}
}

If no payload is received, an empty message will be pushed.

{
   header: { }
   payload: { }
}

If an Array of data is passed, it will be pushed as different messages.

About creating a response

When the pipeline ends, the message payload will be used as the Serverless API result.

If more than one message is emitted from the pipeline, only the payload from the first message is used. If needed, reduce all messages and save them into an array.

Example: The pipeline produces a single, single-object response

Pipeline result:

{
  "header": {},
  "payload": {
     "data": "example data"
   },
   "__type": "ETHOS_MESSAGE"
}

Result when invoked:

{ "data": "example data"}

Example: The pipeline produces an array response

Pipeline result:

{
  "header": {},
  "payload": [
    {
      "data": "1"
    },
    {
      "data": "2"
    }
  ],
  "__type": "ETHOS_MESSAGE"
}

Result when invoked:

[
  {
    "data": "1"
  },
  {
    "data": "2"
  }
]

Incorrect Example: The pipeline produces several messages

In this scenario, only the first result will be returned. A reducer can be used to collect all messages into an array to return. Pipeline result:

[
    {
      "header": {},
      "payload": {
        "data": "1"
      },
      "__type": "ETHOS_MESSAGE"
    },
    {
      "header": {},
      "payload": {
        "data": "2"
      },
      "__type": "ETHOS_MESSAGE"
    }
  ]

Result when invoked:

{
    "data": "1"
}

Validations

The execution endpoint generates exceptions if certain validations are not met.

The following table illustrates known errors and causes.

Error Cause
400 Pipeline configuration error. Parameters might be missing, or be in the wrong format.
401 The token was not sent, the token is not authorized, or the token does not match the specified token type in the pipeline.
403 The provided token is not linked to the appropriate permissions. See Authorization for more details.
404 The pipeline does not exist.
405 HTTP Verb does not match the defined verb in the pipeline.
406 The accept header was not defined or the format is not valid.
406 The specified pipeline version does not exist.
415 The input body does not match the defined input schema.
500 The output message does not match the defined output schema.
500 Pipeline execution error. Usually, the resulting payload will contain a list of errors.

Obtain the current user ID value

A serverless API with an authentication type of 'User token' will inject a property __user.id in the context, with the value being the Ethos Person GUID for the current Experience user.

About this task

This property can be used for different uses cases, for example:

  • Used to fetch data for the current Experience user without requiring the ID to be sent separately.
  • Used for authorization confirmation, for example, that only the current user data is retrieved, or to validate that the current user can access certain data.
  • Call BPAPIs to retrieve a Banner ID as needed.

For example: The following fitting can be used to retrieve the Ethos person that is currently logged into Experience:

"Ethos Proxy Get": {
     "class": "ethosProxyGet",
     "config": {
       "resource": "persons",
       "acceptVersions": [
         "12"
       ],
       "idFromContext": "__user.id",
       "cache": false,
       "ignoreErrors": false,
       "apiKey": "ethosApiKey"
     }
   }

See Ethos Proxy Get fitting.

The value can be retrieved in a JavaScript Transform (JST) fitting by using

context.get('__user').id

Authorization

Grant the permission that allows users to invoke a serverless API that authorizes with a Ethos token or a user (OAuth) token.

Authentication type Ethos token configuration

The serverless API package should be added as an application tag.

Procedure

  1. Navigate to Ethos Integration, then click the Applications tab and select the application that will invoke the serverless API.
    For example, navigate to the Banner Integration application.
  2. Click the Tags sub-tab, then click the Add Tag button. Verify the tag does not already exist.
  3. Enter integration-package as a tag name. The name should match exactly.
  4. As a value, enter the camel-cased version of your displayed package name. This is the Package name and not the serverless API name.
    Examples:
    • A package named 'example' should be added as example (No change).
    • A package named 'Example' should be added as example (The first letter changed case).
    • A package named 'example one' would be added as exampleOne.
    • A package named 'example may 31' would be added as exampleMay31.
  5. If you need more than one integration package to be authorized, add them in the value field separated by a , (comma) with NO spaces between packages.
    Example value: 'example,otherExample,universityPackage'
  6. Click Save. The pipeline is ready to be invoked.
    When executing the serverless API, the presence of a tag with the serverless API's package name is validated. If not present, a 403 HTTP error is returned.
  7. Add the application configured with the integration-package tag to the Application Access list under Platform Components > Data Connect > Application Access.
Authentication type User token configuration

Grant the permission that allows users to invoke a Serverless API that authorizes with a User (OAuth) token. Assign permissions to the specific serverless API.

Before you begin

On the Roles tab in Experience Setup, add the users and roles to whom you want to grant permissions.

Procedure

  1. Access Ellucian Experience Setup:
    1. In the Ellucian Customer Center, click Tools and then select the desired Experience Setup instance under the Experience category:
      • Click Experience Setup to access the Production instance of Experience Setup.
      • Click Experience Setup Test to access the Test instance of Experience Setup.
    2. (If applicable) In Experience Setup, in the Environments drop-down, select the desired Ethos environment.
      The option to select an environment is available only if multiple Ethos environments are associated with this Experience Setup instance.
  2. In the Experience Setup header, click Permissions.
  3. On the Permissions page, click Data Connect.
  4. In the left pane, click the APIs section.
    Expand the APIs section to display:
    • A list of packages that contain serverless APIs.
    • All pipelines within that package that contain serverless APIs.
  5. Assign Execute permissions to the role or user at the desired level:
    • To grant a role or user Execute permissions on all serverless APIs, click APIs.
    • To grant a role or user Execute permissions on the APIs for all pipelines within a package, click the package name.
    • To grant a role or user Execute permissions on the APIs for one pipeline, click the pipeline name.

    For more information about Experience permissions, and the detailed procedure for granting permissions, see Grant Experience application permissions.

  6. Click Save.
  7. In the Confirm Changes to Permissions dialog, review the permissions changes and then click SAVE to complete the process or click CANCEL to go back and modify your selections.
  8. Instruct any user whose permissions have changed to log out of Experience and log back in.
    Experience permissions are cached. Logging out and back in refreshes the cache and ensures that the user has the granted permissions within Experience.
    The pipeline should be callable as an API with the user token that has the appropriate role.

Create schemas

There are two types of schemas in a Serverless API: input and output schemas.

Both schema types follow the same creation process so this guide can be used in either case. Input and output schemas are optional properties within the API Definition object of a pipeline so if not configured, they will not be included in the pipeline JSON object.

Define input and output schemas

When a Serverless API is loaded into the Designer page, it shows the Input Schema and Output Schema tabs. Click on the desired schema to start working with it. The schema definitions can be created, edited, and deleted as long as the Serverless API is in a Draft state.

Input schemas describe the structure of the JSON body sent with a PUT/POST request. Serverless APIs do not support a GET request with a JSON body, and should not have an input schema.

If a schema has not been defined yet, the UI only displays the HTTP method, the Authentication Type of the pipeline, and an empty state message. Any errors detected while working on a schema will be added to the error collection panel located in the top right corner of the UI next to the Test button.

The Payload Type choices for the API output are Object or Array. If the pipeline is configured to return an array, the message should contain an array.

The Payload Type can only be defined when you are configuring an output schema. It is not available in the input schema. If the pipeline is engineered or developed to return an array, then select Array as the Payload Type.

In addition, the Payload Type option is only visible when there is at least one property already defined in the output schema.

Important: Any changes to the schema properties are not saved until the pipeline draft is saved. To do this, click Save.

Add a property

To add a schema property, click the + button located in the left navigation next to Properties.

Doing so will render a form on the main content of the page with the following fields:

Property Name Required This will be used as the property key in the schema object.
Label Optional This field gets parsed to the title schema property.
Property Type Required The simple schema editor allows for Boolean, Date Time,Integer, Number, and String. The Date Time type it will get parsed to a Stringtype and append a Format property with a value of date-time.
Required Optional This property indicates whether the schema property will be mandatory or not.
Description Optional This is used to describe the property.

Fill in the form fields as needed by the property.

Edit a property

To edit an existing property, click the property name in the, located in the left navigation. Alternatively, to edit an existing property, click the More icon and then click Edit.

Delete a property

To delete a property, click the ellipsis icon located next to the property name on the left panel and then click the Delete option. Alternatively, a property can be deleted from the Summary view. Deleting a property from a schema is an action that cannot be undone. However, it will not be completely lost until the pipeline draft is saved. Reloading the browser without saving would result in the property still being displayed.

Summary View

When a schema already has properties, clicking on Summary displays a table listing all the properties and their configuration. You can modify properties by clicking on the corresponding action button on each row. Click the property name in this table to display the form for a property.

The schema is generated dynamically from the UI, and can be seen when exporting the pipeline. Here is an example of a pipeline definition with input and output schemas:

{

  "apiDefinition": {

      "authType": "oauth",

      "httpVerb": "POST",

      "inputSchema": {

        "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-04/schema#",

        "type": "object",

        "properties": {

          "id": {

            "type": "string",

            "title": "GUID",

            "description": "Student GUID"

          },

          "firstName": {

            "type": "string",

            "description": "Student's first name"

          },

          "lastName": {

            "type": "string",

            "description": "Student's last name"

          },

          "finAid": {

            "type": "boolean",

            "title": "Financial Aid",

            "description": "Student has financial aid"

          },

          "registeredOn": {

            "type": "string",

            "format": "date-time",

            "description": "Date on which the student was registered"

          }

        },

        "required": [

          "id",

          "firstName",

          "lastName",

          "registeredOn"

        ]

      },

      "outputSchema": {

        "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-04/schema#",

        "type": "object",

        "properties": {

          "success": {

            "type": "boolean"

          }

        }

      }

    }

}

Return custom HTTP status

The HTTP code and return result can be overridden to enable specific use cases.

For example: A serverless API can return a HTTP status of 404 to indicate a record was not found, or 202 to indicate a process has been started.

By default serverless APIs will return a 200 status and the contents of last message. In case of an error, the returned status code will be 500, with the payload being an array of errors encountered.

The pipeline logic can set the following values in the context to override the returning HTTP code and the resulting content. The values can be set with a JavaScript transform or with a setContext fitting.

  • __httpStatusCode (number) - If set, when you invoke an API Pipeline this value will be used as the HTTP Status code response.
  • __httpStatusMessage (string|object|number) - If set, when you invoke an API Pipeline this value will be used as the HTTP message.
Note: The values can be set one time. Setting the values several times either causes an error, or the values are ignored.

Examples

The following JavaScript function injects values to override both the HTTP status code and the result.

function transform (message, context) {
  context.set("__httpStatusCode", 202);
  context.set("__httpStatusMessage", "Your request has been received");
  message.payload={  message:'hello'}
  return message;
}

An error status code can be specified, as well. You can take advantage of JavaScript transform Stop On Error and throw an error to stop pipeline execution altogether.

function transform (message, context) {
  context.set("__httpStatusCode", 202);
  context.set("__httpStatusMessage", "Your request has been received");
  throw new Error('Error message'); //The pipeline will use the message specified above in the response, so the error message on this line is not actually returned.
}

You can also use a setContext fitting to set the status.

   "Add To Context": {
      "class": "addToContext",
      "config": {
        "source": "$.returnCode",
        "target": "__httpStatusCode"
      }
    },

Execute serverless APIs from Experience extensions

You must execute serverless APIs from Experience extensions.

Prerequisites

  • A serverless API, that specifies User Token as the Authorization Type, should have been published or received by the 'sharing' functionality.
  • Permissions to be enabling calling the Pipeline from an Experience Extension have been set up. Permissions for the API display under Data Connect on the Permissions tab within the Experience Setup page. The user's role needs to be assigned the 'Execute' action for the specific pipeline.
  • An Extension has been created. The extension card can be modified to be able to set a Server Configuration which can be fetched later during the Serverless API. See Define Basic Configuration Parameters documentation for more details.
  • The Extension has been published and enabled to the tenant to execute the Serverless API.

Serverless APIs do not support multiple concurrent threads for processing.

Call a serverless API from a card

To call a serverless API you should use the authenticatedEthosFetch method that is provided by the useData hook from the Experience SDK. This method already injects a valid User Token to the request and an Accept header with the value of 'application/json'.

To optimize performance when calling a Data Connect Serverless API from an Experience Extension, Ellucian recommends including the version in the application/json string, like 'application/vnd.hedtech.integration.v1+json'. Using Semantic Versioning, the card will always call the latest minor version for the major version that is sent. If a new major version is released, the developer will need to update the extension code to call the new major version. An example of how to call a specific version of the API by passing an accept header is shown below:

const response = await authenticatedEthosFetch('my-api', {
            method: 'GET',
            headers: {
                Accept: 'application/vnd.hedtech.integration.v1+json'
            }
        });

Use Server Configuration Card values when calling a Serverless API

You can use Experience's Server Configuration values to store sensitive values, for example, API keys. See Define Basic Configuration Parameters documentation for more details.

It is important to note that whatever you define as a server configuration parameter, the key must match whatever Pipeline Parameters you have defined when designing the serverless API. That is, if you have set a pipeline parameter name to be ethosApiKey, you need to make sure that the same name is set as key on the server configuration object in your extension. Failing to do so would result in that value being ignored by the API execution.

Another important point is that you must include cardId explicitly as a query parameter on the request URI, otherwise, the serverless API will not attempt to get the Server Configuration from your card and continue its execution without it. You can modify the server values when configuring your extension's card in Experience UI but you have to account for two scenarios: calling the API with card configuration, and calling the API with card configuration in preview mode.

Call the API with Card Configuration

Cards within Experience Extensions have a cardId prop set by default. Sending this value as a query parameter on the request made by authenticatedEthosFetch will enable the Serverless API to fetch a Card's Server Configuration value as long as these have been already saved during the Card Configuration process. You can access the cardId prop with the useCardInfo hook provided by the Experience SDK. For example:

import { useData, useCardInfo } from '@ellucian/experience-extension-utils';
const SampleCard = (props) => {
    const { authenticatedEthosFetch } = useData();
 	const { cardId } = useCardInfo();
	const [mydata, setData] = useState();

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchData();
    }, []);

    const fetchData = () => {
        authenticatedEthosFetch(`name-of-your-pipeline-api?cardId=${cardId}`)
            .then((response) => response.json())
            .then((data) => {
                setData(data);
            })
			.catch((error) => {
				// do something with the error
			});
    }

// ...

The above will result in the Serverless API using the saved card configuration values when executing.

Call the API with Card Configuration in Preview Mode

Extensions should account for the scenario in which a Card is being used in a Preview mode.
