This is the result of actively updating the values of the server configuration on the card configuration screen without saving. When using authenticatedEthosFetch on the experience card, the call needs to indicate that its on preview mode, so the server configuration values are retrieved from a temporary storage (these values will not be used on the non-preview mode unless they are explicitly saved on the card configuration process). To enable this behavior, the cardPrefix value of the card needs to be sent as a query parameter, alongside the cardId value on a homonymous query parameter name. All these values are made available by the useCardInfo hook provided by the Experience SDK. For example:

import { useData, useCardInfo } from '@ellucian/experience-extension-utils';
const SampleCard = (props) => {
    const { authenticatedEthosFetch } = useData();
 	const { serverConfigContext: { cardPrefix }, cardId } = useCardInfo();
	const [mydata, setData] = useState();

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchData();
    }, []);

    const fetchData = () => {
        authenticatedEthosFetch(`name-of-your-pipeline-api?cardId=${cardId}&cardPrefix=${cardPrefix}`)
            .then((response) => response.json())
            .then((data) => {
                setData(data);
            })
			.catch((error) => {
				// do something with the error
			});
    }

// ...

The above will result in the serverless API using whatever temporary values from the card configuration for its execution. Combining Server Configuration Card values and Query Params when calling a Serverless API It is possible to use both server configuration card values along with query parameters when executing a serverless API. The query parameter will take precedence over any values returned by the card's configuration. This functionality can be used for testing or for sending non-sensitive values such as dates or flags. For example:

import { useData, useCardInfo } from '@ellucian/experience-extension-utils';
const SampleCard = (props) => {
    const { authenticatedEthosFetch } = useData();
 	const { cardId } = useCardInfo();
	const [mydata, setData] = useState();

    useEffect(() => {
        fetchData();
    }, []);

    const fetchData = () => {
        authenticatedEthosFetch(`name-of-your-pipeline-api?cardId=${cardId}&dateOfBirth=06-07-2023`)
            .then((response) => response.json())
            .then((data) => {
                setData(data);
            })
			.catch((error) => {
				// do something with the error
			});
    }

// ...

Sharing integration pipelines and transform functions

Pipelines and transform functions can be shared with another tenant, if required.

Sharing an artifact will also automatically share the package that the pipeline belongs to, however the shared package in the target tenant will only contain the shared pipelines and transform functions. Unshared artifacts in the original package will not be visible in the target tenant. Only published pipelines can be shared with another tenant.

A shared artifact will appear in the Integration Packages user interface (UI) of the target tenant under the original package name. From here, you can create jobs for the pipeline, however the shared pipeline or transform function will not be available under the Integration Designer for you to edit or use to create drafts. It will only be available in Integration Packages UI.

This only applies to integration pipelines, not serverless APIs. Serverless APIs will not be visible in the Integration Packages card. Serverless APIs that use User Authorization will be visible as resources in Experience Permissions under Integration Packages. APIs that use Ethos tokens will display in the Data Connect platform component.

Major versions of a pipeline are treated as different pipelines; consequently, each major version of the pipeline can be shared separately. Pipelines and transform functions can be shared from the Integration Designer.

Share individual pipelines

You can share a single pipeline.

Procedure

  1. To share, access the Integration Designer. Each version of the published pipeline has a Share pipeline link that is shown when doing click on the three dots icon under Actions tab. This link can be used to view the tenants with which the pipeline has already been shared with and to then share it with additional tenants, if needed.
  2. Clicking on this link will take you to the Pipeline Shared With screen which displays all tenants with which the pipeline has been shared. If the pipeline has not been shared, the Not shared with any tenants message message displays. Click the SHARE button on the upper-right corner to share the pipeline.
  3. Clicking on the SHARE button opens up a Share Pipeline dialog box. This dialog shows a list of tenants that belongs to the current account, will also include all member institutions in the case of a multi-institution account.
  4. Below the name of the pipeline, there is a Search bar that you can use to search within the displayed tenant list by tenant id, tenant name, or account name. You can enter a complete or partial value for any of these identifiers and the table below will be filtered to display the tenants whose tenant ID, name, or account name contains the search string. The search is not case sensitive.
  5. When the search results display, you can select the required tenants from the search results, or if you want to share the pipeline with all tenants that are part of the search results, click Select all search results.
  6. Click Select all search results to select all tenants across multiple pages. If your search has a total of 14 results displayed across three pages, Select all search results selects all 14 available items. To clear the search, click the x Clear icon on the Search bar to display the original tenants list; however, if you selected all or some of your search results, those tenants remain selected as shown by the "number Selected" text at the bottom left corner of dialog.
  7. If you want to share the artifact with all the tenants that belong to your account, you can choose the Select all n option where n is the total number of tenants displayed. You can manually unselect any of the selected tenants or use the CLEAR SELECTION button to clear all your selections. Select All and CLEAR SELECTION only appear in the dialog if you have selected at least one tenant in list already.
  8. When you are satisfied with your selections, click the SHARE button to proceed with sharing the pipeline with the selected tenants.
  9. This action opens up a confirmation dialog that shows a list of your selections so you can verify and confirm that you want to proceed with the share. Click BACK to return to the tenant selection screen and click CANCEL to exit out of the entire process. Click the SHARE button to share the pipeline with the selected tenants.
  10. If sharing is successful, you are returned to the Pipeline Shared With screen where a Pipeline shared successfully message and the tenants that you shared the pipeline with display. If an error occurs during sharing, an error message displays on the screen. This screen also contains a search bar where you can search within the tenants with which the pipeline has been shared.
  11. If you publish a new patch or minor version of the shared pipeline, the tenants that you have already shared the pipeline with do not have the updated version of the pipeline. To ensure that the shared tenants have the latest update of that major version, use the UPDATE ALL button in Pipeline Shared With screen.
    Note: The SHARE button does not appear until you have clicked UPDATE ALL.
  12. Click UPDATE ALL to display a confirmation dialog asking you to confirm the update. Click UPDATE ALL from the confirmation dialog to update the shared tenants with the latest version.
  13. As each major version of the pipeline is considered to be a different pipeline, the update all functionality only becomes available to new patch or minor versions of an already shared major version. For example, if v1.0.0 has been shared, update all is available to all 1.x versions (1.0.1, 1.1.0 and so on). A new major version, such as v2.0.0, is not considered as shared.

Share multiple pipelines

You can share multiple pipelines at the same time.

Procedure

  1. If you want to share multiple pipelines all at once, you can do so from the Integration Designer screen. When selecting a pipeline by clicking on the check box, a share icon displays on the top right corner. Next to the share icon is a CLEAR SELECTION button to clear all selections, a Select All button to select all pipelines, and text showing the number of pipelines selected. Clicking on the share icon opens up the Sharing dialog.
  2. The Sharing dialog is the same as that for sharing individual pipelines. However, in this case the names of all the pipelines that are shared display at the top.
  3. Search for, select, and add tenants in the exact same way as for individual pipelines. When you are done, click SHARE to open the confirmation dialog with the list of selected tenants.
  4. Click the SHARE button to share all the selected pipelines with the selected tenants. A Pipeline shared successfully message displays when sharing is successful. Click Share Pipeline for each pipeline to confirm the share.

Share transform functions

Pipelines and transform functions can be shared with other tenants.

Procedure

  1. The process for sharing transform functions is very similar to pipelines. The link for sharing individual transform functions display when you click the three dots icon under the Actions tab for each transform function. Selecting at least one of the transform functions displays the multiple sharing icon.
  2. Clicking either sharing option displays the share dialog with the tenant selection. Sharing each transform function or multiple transform functions at the same time is exactly the same the pipelines steps.
    Pipeline and transform functions can now be shared with other tenants.

Unshare

There are certain situations, such as when you accidentally share a pipeline to a wrong tenant or discover a critical issue with a shared pipeline, when a pipeline needs to be unshared from a certain tenant. To address this, Designer provides the unsharing feature.

About this task

You have the ability, using the unsharing functionality, to remove previously shared pipelines and transform functions from a target tenant. However, there are some things to take into consideration before unsharing:

  • Ellucian recommends that the target tenants terminate any active or scheduled jobs before unsharing a pipeline from them. Unshare carefully and communicate beforehand.
  • Major versions of a pipeline are treated as different pipelines. Consequently, they are unshared by major version; This means that you can unshare Pipeline 2.X.X but the target tenant can still see and use Pipeline 1.X.X in their Integration Packages UI.
  • When unsharing happens, the unshared pipeline are no longer visible in the Integration Packages UI of the target tenant so they are not able to create more Jobs or make new job runs from it.
  • If no more pipelines and transform functions belonging to the same integration package are left shared in the target tenant, the package is not listed any longer in their Integration Packages UI.
  • Unsharing a transform function can result in unexpected behavior: Transform functions are cached by jobs for up to one (1) hour, and therefore can still be used for some time by an active job.
  • It is not recommended to unshare transform functions before unsharing the pipelines that use them first.

It is important to note that unsharing a pipeline and a transform function are the exact same process, in this example a transform function will be unshared.

Procedure

  1. To unshare, access the Integration Designer screen and select a transform function. Click the three dots icon under the Actions tab and then select Share.
    The Sharing Details screen displays.
  2. All current tenants that the transform function is shared with display in the main table. Select and unshare multiple tenants in one batch or unshare them individually. To unshare in one batch, select the tenants you want to target for unsharing by clicking the check box on the left hand side of the table, and then click on the UNSHARE TRANSFORM FUNCTION button located in the top right corner.
  3. This will prompt a confirmation dialog showing the selected tenants. Click the UNSHARE TRANSFORM FUNCTION button.
  4. This transform function has been successfully unshared from the target tenants. Only this major version of the function has been unshared; other major versions of this function (if shared earlier) are still shared. To unshare any other major version you can repeat this process by selecting that specific version.
  5. Click the UNSHARE TRANSFORM FUNCTION located inside the rows of the main table to unshare the transform function individually.
    Note: This action does not ask for a confirmation and the unshare is done instantly.

Rollback

The rollback feature allows you to remove the last shared version from tenants it was shared with.

Procedure

Any previous versions that were shared will remain intact and users on the shared tenant side will still be able to view and run previous versions. If you need to completely remove a pipeline, see the Unshare process.

Considerations to be taken into account while rolling back a version of the pipeline are similar to that of unsharing:

  • It is recommended that the target tenants terminate any active or scheduled jobs before rolling back a pipeline from them. Rollback should be done carefully and with communication beforehand.
  • If any previous versions of the pipeline were shared with the target tenant, that version will still be visible on the Integration Packages UI of the target tenant.
  • After a rollback, the package may not be listed in the target tenant. If no more pipelines and transform functions, belonging to the same Integration package, are left shared in the target tenant, the package will not be listed any longer in the Data Connect Integration Packages user interface.
  • Use the same process to rollback a transform function.

For example:

  1. Tenant A has shared pipeline version 1.1.0 and 1.1.1 shared with Tenant E.
  2. On Tenant E's Integration Packages UI only the latest version (1.1.1) is visible.
  3. To rollback pipeline v1.1.1, you need to access the Integration Designer screen of the owner tenant (Tenant A). Click the Share Pipeline action of pipeline v1.1.1 to display the Pipeline Shared With screen.
    A ROLLBACK ALL button is present on the top right corner of the screen.
  4. Click the ROLLBACK ALL button to display a confirmation dialog asking you to confirm that this particular version is being rolled back from all shared tenants. You will also be informed that if only this version has been shared, the tenant will no longer have the artifact.
    A Pipeline rolled back from tenants successfully message displays.
  5. When the process completes, the Pipeline Shared with screen displays the UPDATE ALL button, because the older version is still shared with tenants. This is to prompt you to update shared tenants with latest version (v1.1.1).
  6. Now on Tenant E's Integration Packages UI, only the previous version of the shared pipeline (v1.1.0) displays.
  7. The rollback process for the transform function is the same as that of the pipeline.

Share serverless APIs

You can share serverless APIs.

Sharing serverless APIs follows the same general rules as Sharing integration pipelines and transform functions. After a serverless API is shared with a target tenant, it needs to be setup to be called by enabling the proper Authorization according to its type.

Exercises and snippets

Exercise I: Export persons data into a CSV file

To export persons data, it is necessary to configure a pipeline with fittings to collect and format the data, and finally export it into a file.

For this exercise, the first step is to add the ethosApiKey parameter. This parameter is required for some fittings to work.

To add a parameter click on the drop-down menu aside the pipeline name, select Edit Pipeline Settings, and then click the + PARAMETER button.

Set the parameter as required and string type. The name should be ethosAPIKey so the fittings that require it select it by default. If the parameter does not have this specific name, the fittings that require it to have an API key parameter selected from the drop-down, like Ethos Proxy Get, will not work.

If the value for ethosAPIKey is known, it could be added as the default value to avoid setting it every time the pipeline run.

After adding the parameter, the next step is to create the pipeline. For this exercise the fittings needed are:

  • Ethos Proxy Get
  • For each
  • Object Mapper
  • Delimited Formatter
  • Stringify
  • File Writer

Ethos Proxy Get

This fitting is necessary to retrieve all the information of the persons API, which is going to be used to create the CSV. The configuration is simple:

  • Resource field is required, so use persons.
  • Accept version is required, so use the latest, which at the time of writing this document is 12. Write it down and then click the + button.

The response will come with a list of all the persons data adhering to the API schema format. For this exercise, review the schema of the persons API. It is necessary to provide a list of the properties that are wanted or needed in the file, and some of them might not be easily accessible because they are returned inside an array or in children objects.

This fitting is used to apply some modifications to every element in the list. It doesn't require extra configuration for this exercise.

Object mapper

The object mapper is a complex fitting, used to specify which data is required so it can be retrieved from the different properties of each person’s object.

The first property is a particular name from the list of names. The property used to filter the name from the list is preference, so any name in a persons object that has that property, is the one that is added to the file.

The following snippet is a portion of the persons payload:

"names": [
  {
    "firstName": "Pauline",
    "fullName": "Pauline Smith",
    "lastName": "Smith",
    "preference": "preferred",
    "title": "Ms."
  },
  {
    "firstName": "Pauli",
    "fullName": "Pauli Smith",
    "lastName": "Smith",
    "type": {
      "category": "favored"
    }
  }
],

In the first mapping, add the following configuration:

  • Sources -> Path: $.names
  • Target -> Name: _name

Add a transformation function to find the name that contains a property preference with the value preferred for each mapped name, for this, click in the + ADD button at the right of Transformation Functions and then configure it as:

  • Category: array
  • Function: find
  • Enter Parameters: preferred - $.preference (Click + button after entering each parameter)

After defining the names mapping, the content is accessed using the property _name in any of the mappings. You only need to add a reference in the default value, as described in the Object Mapper fitting for mappings.

Create a second mapping to retrieve the value of the firstName property inside _name, for this, click in the + MAPPING button at the end of Mappings section and fill the fields with the next information:

  • Sources -> Default Value: {{mapped._name}}
  • Target -> Name: First Name

It is necessary to create a transformation function for this seccond mapping to retrieve the value from the object, click in the + ADD button at the right of Transformation Functions and use the following:

  • Category: object
  • Function: get
  • Enter Parameters: $.firstName (Click + button after entering this parameter)

To retrieve middleName, lastName and fullName, it is necessary to create additional mappings with the same configuration as for firstName. For this exercise, the target values to be used are "First Name", "Middle Name", "Last Name" and "Full Name".

There might be cases where additional information is needed from a different part of the object or that require a certain format. For this example, three more properties will be retrieved: dateOfBirth, ethnicity and race.

Because dateOfBirth is a property that is accessible in the first level, it can be retrieved directly, however, a different format to the date is going to be used so it looks more user friendly. To do that, it is necessary to use a Transformation Function for date.

As described in the documentation, the transformation function category for date accepts input and output date format strings based on Moment.js Format documentation, so it will transform the date from "YYYY-MM-DD" to a "MMMM Do, YYYY" format by adding those parameters (the order is important).

Create a new map and fill the fields with the following information:

  • Sources -> Path: $.dateOfBirth
  • Target -> Name: Date Of Birth

And a transform function for the map with the following:

  • Category: date
  • Function: format
  • Enter Parameters: MMMM Do, YYYY - YYYY-MM-DD (Click + button after entering each parameter)

The next value from persons to be mapped is ethnicity. The code snippet shows the portion of the payload that contains it:

"ethnicity": {
  "ethnicGroup": {
    "id": "7582a6e5-328b-489b-9b28-6fdf7b555b89"
  },
  "reporting": [
    {
      "country": {
        "code": "USA",
        "ethnicCategory": "nonHispanic"
      }
    }
  ]
}

For this exercise, the ethnicCategory value is retrieved. To do that, another mapping is added with the next information in the fields (note that we are using full path as source):

  • Sources -> Path: $.ethnicity.reporting[0].country.ethnicCategory
  • Target -> Name: Ethnicity

The last mapping is for races, and like the names property, the races property is an array.

"races": [
  {
    "race": {
      "id": "598b3e89-544a-4a13-80a2-a1b7fca69d02"
    },
    "reporting": [
      {
        "country": {
          "code": "USA",
          "racialCategory": "asian"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
]

For this example, instead of filtering a particular race, like what was done with names, all the races the person has assigned will be retrieved and then concatenated using a “|” symbol.

The first step is to define the full path to get the racial category of every race object in the array. Create a new map and use:

  • Sources -> Path: $.races[*].reporting[0].country.racialCategory
  • Target -> Name: Race

The xpath definition used will return an array of racialCategories, so it is necessary to add a transformation function to concatenate or join the values. Add a transform function with:

  • Category: array
  • Function: join
  • Enter Parameters: | (Click + button after entering the parameter)

Delimited formatter

The delimited formatter is the fitting used to create the final format for the CSV, here is where the mapped properties created by the object mapper will be used.

This fitting has certain levels of customization for header, footer, and details, however for this exercise, only the details are going to be described. To do this, it is required to use the names of the properties and the mapped data that was created.

Most of the properties were already mapped using the object mapper, the target value of each of those mappings can be assigned to path so it can get the data, however, gender is a property that hasn't been mapped, it is contained in the original object, therefore the label Gender will be used as column header.

In the Details section, turn on the Column Headers check-box, your columns should look like this:

  • Path: First Name
  • Path: Middle Name
  • Path: Last Name
  • Path: Full Name
  • Path: gender, Label: Gender
  • Path: Ethnicity
  • Path: Race
  • Path: Date Of Birth

Running the pipeline using the RUN TEST button will retrieve all the persons data in a comma separated list of payloads.

The final step is to generate the CSV file, however each of the payloads that are going to be written to the file need to be transformed into a string, and then use a File Writer.

Stringify

This fitting doesn’t need any configuration. It is only necessary to add it after the Delimited Formatter to 'stringify' the JSON payloads.

File writer

This fitting will allow the pipeline to create a file into Ellucian cloud storage.

The only necessary input is the name of the file. Because it contains a list of persons information, the option Add Newline After Each Message will be set to ON or true. The option Generate Presigned Url should be set to ON or true too, so the payload will retrieve the presigned URL to get the file.

Finally, run the pipeline by clicking the RUN TEST button to verify everything works as intended.

Copy the URL in the payload and paste it in a browser to verify the CSV file was created with all the expected data.

Exercise II: Import persons data from a CSV file

You can import a CSV file that contains persons data and convert it to a JSON file.

The first thing needed is to configure the pipeline parameters. For this exercise, two parameters are required.

  • The first one is going to be fileName, of type file.
  • the second is going to be dateSeparator, of type string.

The purpose of fileName is to allow you to upload a local file to the S3 bucket, so it can be used as the input data. The file used is the same file that was created with the example file generated in Exercise I: Export persons data into a CSV file.

The second parameter, dateSeparator, is added to give an example of how to use context parameters in a JavaScript transform fitting. The default value for this parameter is a ",".

After configuring the parameters for the pipeline, The next step is to add and configure the fittings.

The fittings used for this exercise are:

  • JavaScript Transform
  • Add to Context
  • File Reader
  • Line Parser
  • Delimited Parser
  • Object Mapper
  • Stringify
  • File Writer

JavaScript Transform (Date)

The first fitting is used to add a datetime record to know when the file was imported. The main purpose of this fitting in the exercise is to show how to add values to the context so they can be used later. The data can come from any resource, either use an Ethos Proxy GET to retrieve some data, read a file, add a new variable, etcetera.

This fitting is used to inject the date into the payload. Set the parameter name as dateNow:

function transform (message, context) {
  // Put your code here.
  message.payload.dateNow = Date.now();
  return message;
}

Add to Context

Add to context is a simple fitting. It only provides a way to insert a value to the context from the payload so the configuration is easy. Use $.dateNow as the Source and _importDate as the Target. The fitting takes the dateNow value and creates a context parameter named _importDate.

File Reader

The file reader is a fitting used to retrieve the data of a file from the store.

The configuration of the File Reader requires only the name of the file in the Key field.

There are a couple of methods to add the file name, the first one is by using {{context.fileName}}.

If this method is used, you have to select the file (using the file parameter) every time to upload it to the store, then the file reader uses that name to find and retrieve the file.

The second method is to provide a specific file name in the configuration, like file.csv.

By doing it this way, selecting the file every time after the first time is not necessary. The file needs to be uploaded one time so that the file reader can find it, it won't be necessary to do it anymore as long as the file (with that name) exists in the store. If the file does not exist, the response will contain an error like this:

{
  "status": 200,
  "statusText": "",
  "data": [],
  "runId": "a78a47b5-0a1b-4f82-a699-38e9b59fd789",
  "errors": [
    {
      "severity": "Warning",
      "responseCode": 404,
      "description": "f72efbe7-723a-4c2e-a8bf-1f01fc4e99c1/Excersice01-fb895201-c65a-415f-8e969fec7425f.csv (NoSuchKey)",
      "details": "The specified key does not exist.",
      "correlationId": "a78a47b5-0a1b-4f82-a699-38e9b59fd789"
    }
  ]
}

Line Parser

The line parser is a fitting that will split the payload into multiple messages for each new line character it finds. The line parser fitting does not need any configuration.

Delimited Parser

The delimited parser is a fitting that will format the message that comes either in a tab or comma delimited data into a JavaScript object.

The delimited parser configuration has an optional property named Target that can be used to place the output array, however this exercise is not going to use it.

The delimited parser assumes that the first line it receives is the header line, so the CSV file that was used works perfectly with this fitting. It will format the message into an array of JavaScript objects.

JavaScript Transform (Data)

This is the second JavaScript transform fitting used for this exercise. This time, the fitting will change some of the data.

The first part of the function reassigns the data to other object properties that are in a camelCase format.

The second part formats the Date of Birth. In the CSV file, the date was in a "MMMM Do, YYYY" format. This means the month is in full text and the day is an ordinal number like June 1st, 2010, however this value cannot be used to create a date so it is necessary to format it.

First, the dateSeparator parameter, which was defined as a comma for this exercise, is taken from the context and used to split the date string, this will return an array with two values (June 1st) and (2010), and then the values are concatenated to get August 13 1977. Finally, create a new Date object and convert it to a string following the ISO 8601 Extended Format.

function transform (message, context) {
  const data = message.payload;
  let newPayload = {};
  newPayload.firstName = data['First Name'];
  newPayload.middleName = data['Middle Name'];
  newPayload.lastName = data['Last Name'];
  newPayload.fullName = data['Full Name'];
  newPayload.gender = data['Gender'];
  newPayload.race = data['Race'];
  newPayload.ethnicity = data['Ethnicity'];
  
  // The date of birth comes in a "month cardinalDay, year" format,
  // so we are going to transform it into a local String format.
  let dateStr = data['Date Of Birth'];
  newPayload.dateOfBirth = '';
  if(dateStr) {
    // An example of how to use context values defined as our pipeline parameters.
    let dateArr = dateStr.split(context.get('dateSeparator'));
    // Format the date to change from ordinal to cardinal number for the days.
    let newDate = dateArr[0].substring(0, dateArr[0].length - 2).concat(dateArr[1]);
    newPayload.dateOfBirthFormated = newDate;
    newPayload.dateOfBirth = new Date(newDate).toISOString();
  }
  
  newPayload.oldData = data;
  message.payload = newPayload;
  return message;
}

In this step of the test, the original data of the payload (oldData), and the formatted date of birth (dateOfBirthFormatted) are assigned to the new object, the purpose is to show the changes, however both will be removed after this step. The payload now has the dateOfBirth formatted and ready.

"payload": {
  "firstName": "test B",
  "middleName": "A",
  "lastName": "Barrens",
  "fullName": "test B A Barrens",
  "gender": "male",
  "race": "",
  "ethnicity": "",
  "dateOfBirth": "1977-08-13T00:00:00.000Z",
  "dateOfBirthFormated": "August 13 1977",
  "oldData": {
    "First Name": "test B",
    "Middle Name": "A",
    "Last Name": "Barrens",
    "Full Name": "test B A Barrens",
    "Gender": "male",
    "Ethnicity": "",
    "Race": "",
    "Date Of Birth": "August 13th, 1977"
  }
}

Object Mapper

The object mapper is used to map some properties in the payload.

The first mapping uses the _importDate parameter that was added to the context before and adds to each object in the array of payloads:

  • Sources -> Default Value: {{context._importDate}}
  • Target -> Name: importDate

After that, add a transformation function that converts the date to a YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss.SSS string format:

  • Category: date
  • Function: format
  • Enter Parameters: YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss:SSS (Click + button after entering the parameter)

    Enter Parameters: YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss:SSS (Click + button after entering the parameter)

Add a second mapping, this adds a new property, named ethnicityCode, to the object:

  • Sources -> Path: $.ethnicity
  • Target -> Name: ethnicityCode

This time, the exercise shows how to use crosswalks to customize some translation values, it also enables you to set a default code value in case the ethnicity comes with an empty value. The name of this crosswalk is ethinicityCrw. Add a transform function with the following values:

  • Category: util
  • Function: crosswalk
  • Enter Parameters: ethinicityCrw (Click + button after entering the parameter)

In the crosswalk section, click in the + CROSSWALK button to create the mappings for the crosswalk. In this exercise, two source values will be mapped: hispanic and nonHispanic, for anything else the ethnicityCode is going to have UNK as the value. Configure your crosswalk as follows:

  • Crosswalk Name: ethinicityCrw
  • Default: UKN
  • Mapping01:
    • Mapping Name: non hispanic
    • Target Value: NONHSPNC
    • Source Value: nonHispanic
  • Mapping02:
    • Mapping Name: hispanic
    • Target Value: HSPNC
    • Source Value: hispanic

After the test runs, the response contains the two new properties added to each object. In this snippet, there is a case where a code is mapped correctly and a case where the ethnicity is empty and therefore is using the default value.

"payload": {
  "firstName": "Charles",
  "middleName": "",
  "lastName": "Block",
  "fullName": "Charles Block",
  "gender": "male",
  "race": "",
  "ethnicity": "nonHispanic",
  "dateOfBirth": "",
  "importDate": "2023-03-15 16:45:55:496",
  "ethnicityCode": "NONHSPNC"
}
"payload": {
  "firstName": "Pamela",
  "middleName": "Susan",
  "lastName": "Smithy",
  "fullName": "Pamela Susan Smithy",
  "gender": "female",
  "race": "",
  "ethnicity": "",
  "dateOfBirth": "1965-02-27T00:00:00.000Z",
  "importDate": "2023-03-15 16:45:55:496",
  "ethnicityCode": "UKN"
},

Stringify

Stringify is added to transform the payloads to JSON strings so that they can be used later by file writer. It does not need any configuration.

File Writer

This fitting creates a file in Ellucian cloud storage.

To configure the file writer, the name is necessary. In this exercise the file name will be personsImportFromCsv.json. Switch the Generate Presigned Url feature to ON or true so the response contains the URL to download the file.

Both Add Newline After Each Message and Include Total Count are optional, for this exercise set both switches ON or true. The first configuration makes the JSON file more readable, the second option includes the total count in the response.

Finally, test the pipeline to verify that the file is created. Copy the presignedUrl and paste it in a browser to get the JSON file and verify that the data is correct.

Exercise III: HTML Formatter fitting example

You can use the HTML Formatter fitting to create HTML output that includes data gathered from one or more sources associated to the institution.

Before you begin

This example requires you to provide a JSON file as input when the pipeline is run, and that JSON file is to have the data that will be parsed by the HTML template Mustache expressions.

Under other use case scenarios, it is possible the data will come from GET API calls in the pipeline, made before running the HTML fitting, so the file as input is referenced here for example purposes.

About this task

When the pipeline is run, it uses the information provided as part of the HTML template, processes any Mustache tags, replaces them with the provided data, and produces HTML output that can be saved as a target file.

See HTML Formatter fitting for a description of the HTML Formatter fitting.

For more information on Mustache tag expressions, see https://mustache.github.io/mustache.5.html.

Procedure

  1. From the Experience dashboard, use either of these methods to access the Integration Designer page:
    • From the Application menu:
      1. Click the Applications icon in the Experience navigation area and then click Integration Designer.
      2. On the Packages page, in the left pane, click the integration package this new pipeline will be in.
    • From the Integration Designer card (if supported at your institution):
      1. Click the Integration Designer card.
      2. On the Integration Designer card on the Experience dashboard, click the integration package this new pipeline will be in.
  2. An Integration Designer package should contain pipelines that relate to each other. If necessary, create a new package.
    1. To create a new package, click + in the Packages section of the Integration Designer.
    2. Create a unique name for the package.
    3. Optional: Add a description of the package contents.
    4. Click Save.
    5. Select the package you just created in the list of packages to continue.
  3. In the package, create a new pipeline.
    1. In the Pipelines section of the Integration Designer, click + PIPELINE to create a new pipeline.
    2. Enter a unique name for the pipeline.
    3. Optional: Add a description for this pipeline.
    4. Click Save to save the pipeline.
  4. In the Integration Designer for your new pipeline, click More next to the pipeline name.
  5. Select Edit Pipeline Settings.
  6. Click + PARAMETER to add the parameter to allow you to upload a JSON data file each time the pipeline is run.
  7. Define the new parameter to upload the file.
    1. Enter a unique name for this parameter.
      The parameter name must be a single word starting with a letter, dollar sign, or underscore, and cannot have any special characters.
    2. Set Label and Default to None (default).
    3. Enable Required.
    4. Disable Sensitive (default).
    5. Change Type to File.
    6. Click Add Parameter.
      Next, you will add the necessary fittings to the pipeline: File Reader, Reducer, JSON Parser, HTML Formatter, and File Writer.
  8. Add a File Reader fitting.
    This will retrieve the contents of the file that will be provided when the pipeline is run.
    1. In the side menu, click Sources to open the list of fittings that consume data.
    2. Click File Reader to add a File Reader fitting to the pipeline.
      For additional information about this fitting, refer to File Reader fitting.
    3. Click the new File Reader fitting to open the details pane.
    4. Optional: Replace the default fitting name (File Reader) with a descriptive name.
    5. Optional: Add a description for this fitting.
    6. Enter the file name in the Key field.
      The file name must be all lowercase letters and should match the name of the file that will be provided when the pipeline runs.
    7. If uploading a local file, do not select any values for Bucket, Access Key ID, or Secret Access Key.
    8. Click Save to save the segment.
  9. Add a Reducer fitting.
    This will ensure the full contents of the file are accumulated and passed along as a single message to the rest of the pipeline fittings.
    1. In the side menu, click Destinations to open the list of fittings that send data to an end state.
    2. Click Reducer to add a Reducer fitting to the pipeline.
      As part of the reducer, you can specify which property will include the captured data and pass it along to the next fitting. You can specify the default payload property as the accumulator See Reducer fitting.
    3. Click the new Reducer fitting to open the details pane.
    4. Optional: Replace the default fitting name (Reducer) with a descriptive name.
    5. Optional: Add a description for this fitting.
    6. Required: Enter a value in the accumulator field.

      This is the property in the new payload upon which to set the accumulated array of payloads.

      For this example, save this back to the payload property. See the reference in the HTML Formatter fitting to the message.payload in Mustache.

    7. Click Save to save the segment.
  10. Add a JSON Parser fitting.
    At this moment, the JSON file contents are in string format, so the JSON object needs to be restored. To achieve this, include a JSON Parser fitting.
    1. In the side menu, click Transformations to open the list of fittings that transform data.
    2. Click JSON Parser to add a JSON Parser fitting to the pipeline.
      For additional information about this fitting, refer to JSON Parser fitting.
    3. Click the new JSON Parser fitting to open the details pane.
    4. Optional: Replace the default fitting name with a descriptive name.
    5. Optional: Add a description for this fitting.
    6. The fitting accepts any type of incoming message, but will only parse one that has a JSON string payload.
    7. Click Save to save the segment.
  11. Add a HTML Formatter fitting.
    As part of the template property, include any HTML content you want the fitting to process, including Mustache tag references to the data that is being passed along.
    1. In the side menu, click Transformations to open the list of fittings that transform data.
    2. Click HTML Formatter to add a HTML Formatter fitting to the pipeline.
      For additional information about this fitting, refer to HTML Formatter fitting.
    3. Click the new HTML Formatter fitting to open the details pane.
    4. Optional: Replace the default fitting name with a descriptive name.
    5. Optional: Add a description for this fitting.
    6. Required: Enter a value in the Template field.
      This is HTML content with or without Mustache expressions. If payload data is referenced from the Mustache tags, ensure the tags reference the full structure, such as {{message.payload.field}} or the corresponding property where the JSON data objects are stored.
    7. Click Save to save the segment.
    After the pipeline processes the HTML content and replaces any Mustache tag placeholders, a File Writer fitting can capture this output and generate a file for it.
  12. Add a File Writer fitting.
    1. In the side menu, click Destinations to open the list of fittings that send data to an end state.
    2. Click File Writer to add a File Writer fitting to the pipeline.
      For additional information about this fitting, refer to File Writer fitting.
    3. Click the new File Writer fitting to open the details pane.
    4. Optional: Replace the default fitting name with a descriptive name.
    5. Optional: Add a description for this fitting.
    6. Enter a File Name for the output HTML file name.
    7. Optional: For testing purposes, you might want to select Generate Presigned Url to configure the File Writer to generate a presigned URL with the output for the file.
    8. Configure Bucket, Access Key ID, or Secret Access Key information as needed for a target location, or leave this information blank so the file can be downloaded from the job run page as needed.
    9. Click Save to save the segment.
  13. Click Save to save the pipeline.
    Your pipeline should look similar to this example.

  14. Optional: Test the pipeline, providing a JSON file as input that matches the data structure the HTML template is expecting.
    1. While viewing your new pipeline in the Integration Designer, click Test.
    2. Click Upload File and select the input JSON file.
    3. Optional: Enable Enable Diagnostic log to generate a diagnostic log for this pipeline execution.
      The log file will be available after the test completes. Refer to Enable diagnostics logs in Troubleshooting for more details.
    4. Click RUN TEST.
    5. When the test completes, review the results.
      The Raw tab result displays by default.

      Results display for the last segment executed. See the log file for test results for other segments in the pipeline.

      If the test is unsuccessful, review your fittings setup and refer to Troubleshooting for more assistance.

    6. If you turned on the Generate Presigned Url property on the File Writer, the Raw output of the test will include the URL with the location of the HTML file that was generated. Copy and paste this address (without the quotes) in another window in your browser to see the contents of the file, and verify it is the output that you expected.
    For more details about the Test process and overall publishing process, see Publish integration pipelines.
  15. Publish the pipeline.
    1. Click Publish.
    2. Select a release version to publish.
    3. Click Publish.
  16. Access the Integration Packages card from Data Connect. Ensure permissions have been granted for your user in Experience Setup so that the new pipeline is available. See Integration Designer overview.
  17. Select the new pipeline you just published and click + New Job to create a new job.
    1. Enter a job name.
    2. Click Upload File and provide a JSON file as input that matches the data structure the HTML template is expecting.
    3. Leave Run Now selected (default).
    4. Click Save to run the job.
  18. If there is an error while the Data Connect job is running, review the Data Connect logs.
    See Common questions.

Snippet: Crosswalk setup

You can set up a global crosswalk.

This is a simple example of setting up a global crosswalk. See Develop pipelines: Crosswalks.

Refer to Object Mapper fitting documentation for more Crosswalk configuration details.

For this example, you can work with the following input:

[
  {"name":"Jim", "lastName":"Hawkins", "job": "Cabin boy" },
  {"name":"Long John","lastName":"Silver", "job": "Pirate" },
  {"name":"David","lastName":"Livesey", "job": "Doctor" }
]
You will create a crosswalk that will translate job into a generic codes: SEA_BASED, EARTH_BASED.
  1. First create the crosswalk in the Crosswalks page. Click Crosswalks in the navigation menu within the Integration Packages extension.
  2. Click on + after List of Crosswalks to add a new crosswalk, for this exercise, we will name it jobCrosswalk
  3. Use the presented screen to create mappings.
  4. Use {{input}} as the Default Target Value. This value will cause the original input to be used if no match is found.
    Note: The Mapping Name is free form, Target Value defines the output code and Source Values can be a list with values that the engine will match on the input.

For this example, use the next mappings:

  • Mapping01:
    • Mapping Name: earth job code
    • Target Value: EARTH_BASED
    • Source Value: Doctor
  • Mapping02:
    • Mapping Name: sea job code
    • Target Value: SEA_BASED
    • Source Value: Pirate

This concludes the crosswalk setup. In the next step you will configure a small pipeline to use the crosswalk.

Create a new pipeline and add a Object Mapper fitting

Crosswalks can be defined in the Object Mapper itself, or as a global crosswalk as previously shown, and are called through the transformation functions.

Under the Mappings sections, configure the first mapping as follows:

  • Sources -> Path: $.job
  • Target -> Name: jobCode

And add a transform function with the next configuration (the entered parameter must be the crosswalk name):

  • Category: util
  • Function: crosswalk
  • Enter Parameters: jobCrosswalk (Click + button after entering the parameter)

Test the pipeline, add the JSON input data provided at the beginning of this page and click RUN TEST. The output should look like this:

{
  "status": 200,
  "statusText": "",
  "data": [
    {
      "header": {},
      "payload": {
        "name": "Jim",
        "lastName": "Hawkins",
        "job": "Cabin boy",
        "jobCode": "Cabin boy"
      },
      "__type": "ETHOS_MESSAGE"
    },
    {
      "header": {},
      "payload": {
        "name": "Long John",
        "lastName": "Silver",
        "job": "Pirate",
        "jobCode": "SEA_BASED"
      },
      "__type": "ETHOS_MESSAGE"
    },
    {
      "header": {},
      "payload": {
        "name": "David",
        "lastName": "Livesey",
        "job": "Doctor",
        "jobCode": "EARTH_BASED"
      },
      "__type": "ETHOS_MESSAGE"
    }
  ],
  "runId": "29f90586-e663-4dbe-b28f-2585bd5f3913"
}

Snippet: How to retrieve nested data from payload

There might be cases when you need to collect data from different arrays or properties in a JSON response. For these cases, Ellucian recommends to first find the information that you want to retrieve. Try retrieving the names from the persons resource.

After calling the resource, the response is returned with something similar to:

"names": [
  {
    "firstName": "Katherine",
    "fullName": "Katherine Jenkins",
    "lastName": "Jenkins",
    "preference": "preferred",
    "title": "Ms."
  },
  {
    "firstName": "Kate",
    "fullName": "Kate Jenkins",
    "lastName": "Jenkins",
    "type": {
      "category": "favored"
    }
  }
],

The objective is to retrieve the preferred name, so it is necessary to create an Object Mapper (If there are multiple objects, you must create a For Each fitting before the Object Mapper), define a mapping and a function.

Path is a JSONPath so, the mapping requires to define the path and a target name:

  • Sources -> Path: $.names
  • Target -> Name: Name

If the test is run like this, the response will contain the whole array defined in names, so a transformation function is required. The function find requires you first define the value and then the property in the parameters list:

  • Category: array
  • Function: find
  • Enter Parameters: preferred - $.preference (Click + button after entering each parameter)

The response payload contains the object that preference value was preferred.

This can also be refined by adding an extra transform function to collect only the firstName:

  • Category: object
  • Function: get
  • Enter Parameters: firstName (Click + button after entering the parameter)

The response payload retrieves the expected value: "Name": "Katherine".

How-to's, Patterns, Recipes, and Ideas

Provides information about pipeline errors.

Error handling on Pipelines

During the design phase, any errors that arise during pipeline execution are reported immediately as part of the test runner pop up. This contrasts with a published pipeline, where the error status is reported and then you can click on Errors to jump to the Errors tab.
  • An error during design phase: If a pipeline throws an error during testing in design phase, an Errors tab will appear next to Payloads tab in the Test Pipeline dialog.
  • An error during a job run phase:
    • The pipeline runs as scheduled, but fails. The error is reported in the job status page and in the details.
    • You can click on View Errors, for a specific job to display the Errors Report tab, already setup to filter by Job Run ID (also known as Correlation ID).
    • The more details button on the far right can be used to view more information about the error.

Error patterns

Some fittings have specific configuration for errors. For example, they can store the error from a request to be processed later or they can stop the pipeline execution altogether. Refer to each fitting documentation for further detail. Unless specified, an error will stop the pipeline for the given message, not the whole workflow.

The following are usage ideas.

Save error for later processing

This segment posts information to persons and stores data in errors:
"Ethos Proxy Post": {
  "class": "ethosProxyPost",
  "config": {
    "resource": "academic-levels",
    "contentVersion": "6",
    "acceptVersion": "6",
    "errorPath": "errors"
  }
}
This segment evaluates if the POST call returned errors and provides appropriate error messages by adding a new property to the original payload:
"JavaScript Transform": {
  "class": "JavaScriptTransform",
  "config": {
    "pushUndefined": true,
    "stopOnError": false,
    "code": "function transform (message, context) {\n  if(message.errors.code == \"key_already_exists\"){\n    message.payload.errorMessage =\"Key already exists\"\n  }\n  \n  if(message.errors.code == \"invalid_level\"){\n    message.payload.errorMessage =\"The level is invalid, check dependencies\"\n  }\n  \n  return message;\n}\n"
  }
}

Stop On Error condition with JavaScript transform

This segment evaluates a message and then stops pipeline execution altogether by throwing an exception. Any new messages are dropped, effectively stopping the pipeline. If the pipeline has been split into phases for parallel processing, this might not stop the pipeline, any such evaluation is done on the fan-in portion of the pipeline. Refer to the performance section for more information on parallel processing.

Access an error response HTTP status

Given a segment that performs an HTTP request (GET, POST, PUT, etc), any error that arises is saved to the defined Error Path field. for this example, we will use errors. An error will also report an "Error", which will mark the pipeline as "Failed". On error, the following payload is returned:

{
  "payload": {
    "errors": {
      "code": 404,
      "body": {
        "statusCode": 404,
        "description": "Not Found"
      }
    }
  }
}

Additional logic can check for the status using the payload.errors.code property.

Common patterns

The following are common patterns to address common problems.

Concurrency

  • Pipeline doesn't use forEach- how can I change it?:
    • Apply the reducer fitting, then add forEach. For example, if the pipeline is reading 1000 person IDs from a file, and then fetching a record from Ethos for each person.
    • Sample:
      File Reader → Line Parser → Ethos Proxy Get
      Can be changed to this to add parallelism:
      File Reader → Line Parser → Reducer → forEach → Ethos Proxy Get
  • For a phase to run in parallel, it can only use the following fittings:
    • Add to Context
    • Ethos Proxy fittings
    • Ethos GraphQL
    • JavaScript Transform
    • JSON Parser
    • Merge
    • Object Mapper
    • File Attributes
    • SFTP List
    • Stringify
  • Context vs. Message Header:
    • The Context use case is to store information used repeatedly and that cannot be overwritten, for example, school codes, general codes, etc.
    • The Message header is intended to store information pertaining to the message, for example, calculated student codes, person information, etc.
    • Here is an example workflow of "Add to context":
      EthosProxyGet.- Retrieve current Term → AddToContext.- Save Term to Context → EthosProxyGetArray.- Retrieve Persons → ObjectMapper.- Uses Term for all Persons → ...
      Note: The total amount of data stored in pipeline context is limited to 2.5 GB per execution. This includes data added using the Add to Context fitting. If the limit is exceeded, the pipeline execution fails with a clear error message.
    • An example of a workflow using header:
      EthosProxyGetArray.- Retrieve Persons → ForEach → EthosProxyGet.- Retrieve Persons address. Target: payload.header.zipCode = address.zipCode → ObjectMapper.- Uses Payload + header → ...
  • Consecutive loops using intermediate files:
    • The pipeline might need to loop through the same payload over and over. For example, a pipeline might need to create aggregate data from persons and addresses, update some data, write a report, create a CSV, followed by creating an XML, etc. One common problem is that writing to a file outputs data about the result file, and the original message data is lost. Instead of calling the API again (and any intermediate data to create the payload) the pattern is to write the payload to an intermediate file, then reading that file repeatedly, effectively caching the work done.
    • The following example shows how the data is created, stored in a file, and then read two times: one time to post data for update and a second time to create a report. More calls can be chained by using the same read-then-apply pattern.
      EthosProxyGetArray.- Retrieve Persons → ForEach → EthosProxyGet.- Retrieve Persons address. Target - payload.header.zipCode = address.zipCode → ObjectMapper.- Uses Payload + header → Stringify → s3Sink.- Creates an intermediate file that can be read multiple times. Will write a file to {job run id}/filename.json → s3Accessor.- "key": "{pipelineName}/{{context.runId}}/filename.json" → EthosProxyPost.- Update Persons → s3Accessor.- "key": "{pipelineName}/{{context.runId}}/filename.json" → s3Sink.- Updates Persons Report → ...

Externalize JavaScript transform functions

A JS Transform function can also be externalized so it can be referenced any time in a pipeline for any amount of times without having to rewrite the function every time you want to use it.

Even better, externalizing a function can make it available to use in any pipeline within a specific pipeline. See Develop pipelines.

Previously, Develop pipelines: JavaScript Transform Functions were shown for error handling at an inline level, meaning they are written in the fitting configuration and only available when that fitting is executed.

Additionally, externalized JS Transform Functions can be versioned, so bug fixes or additional logic can be introduced with ease.

Create a JavaScript transform function draft

In order to externalize a function, you must first create a draft. You can update and test the drafts within the Designer.

About this task

A pipeline draft will not be published if it references a function draft rather than a published function.

Procedure

  1. To create a transform function draft, click on an existing package inside the Integration Designer screen. Then click on the Transform Functions tab, and then the + TRANSFORM FUNCTION button on the right side of the screen.
  2. Enter a Transform Function to have a globally unique name and a valid syntax. After you complete these fields, click the SAVE button to create a draft.
  3. To test the Transform Function draft in the Designer, add a JavaScriptTransform fitting and select an Artifact Name in the configuration.
    This drop-down shows all available Transform Functions within the Integration Package; including drafts and published functions. In this example, the Draft tag is added. The fitting configuration also displays the function’s content but it will not allow edits.
Edit an existing JavaScript transform function draft

Transform function drafts can be edited before publishing and this can be done any amount of times.

Procedure

  1. To edit a draft, click on the ellipsis belonging to the draft you want to edit and then select the Edit option from the menu.
  2. This will prompt a dialog where you can update the Transform Function. To change the name, Ellucian recommends deleting the draft and creating a new one. After making the changes, click SAVE.
Delete a JavaScript transform function draft

A transform function can be deleted as long as it is not currently shared or is in draft state.

Procedure

  1. To delete a function, open the Actions menu button and select the Delete option.
  2. A confirmation dialog displays. Click the DELETE button.
  3. After the function is deleted, update all references to this function in the pipelines that currently use it. Otherwise, a pipeline test or run can result in unexpected behavior or error out.
Publish a JavaScript transform function

The publishing process of a transform function is similar to the one of a pipeline, with the only difference that publishing a transform function is done directly from the Integration Designer main screen.

Procedure

  1. Open the Actions menu button and select the Publish option.
  2. Optional: In the dialog, versioning is left to the user’s discretion. The next Patch and Minor versions options are displayed in addition to the next Major version. Versioning works the same as in pipelines. Patch and minor versions of a function are consolidated and only the latest is shown in the Integration Designer Transform Function table, while the major version will be treated as a completely different Transform Function, hence showing as another row in the Integration Designer Transform Function table.
  3. After you select a version, click the PUBLISH button.
  4. You can now test the transform function in a pipeline and it is available at an integration package level.
    There is a Published tag next to the function’s name and the option to select a fixed Artifact Version is enabled.
Considerations when using an externalized JavaScript transform function

Describes considerations when using an externalized JavaScript Transform Function.

Some considerations to take into account when using an externalized Transform Function are that externalized-based scripts are cached for faster repeated execution and the retrieval only happens one time per pipeline execution. Knowing that, when choosing to use the latest version of a Transform Function inside the JavaScriptTransform fitting configuration, it should be used carefully because updating a Transform Function and publishing a new version of it can result in undesirable behavior ad hoc for ongoing Pipeline Jobs executions that use the configuration.

In addition, publishing a pipeline that uses an external Transform Function does not automatically publish the function. The Transform Function needs to be published separately.

Troubleshooting

Troubleshooting tips are provided.

Enable diagnostics logs

When testing a pipeline, you can toggle the Enable diagnostic log option to generate a log file after execution. After the test pipeline executes, an icon at the bottom will allow downloading the log file.

A log file is not generated if the pipeline test exceeds the maximum execution time of 2 minutes.

A generated log file contains detailed information on the input and output of each pipeline segment, as they are executed. The file information is in JSON format.

For example, a log file can contain:

  • Timestamp and type of fitting being executed.
  • Values assigned to context during pipeline initialization.
  • Output message of a fitting.

For more information on Diagnostic logging of Integration Packages pipeline jobs, please refer to the Integration Packages documentation.

Troubleshooting ideas

  • When testing, be advised that the pipeline may only execute for 60 seconds. Limit your data to a small number of records using filters or other parameters so that the pipeline can complete.
  • Disable fittings to find the problem:

    Whenever there is an issue with a pipeline, Ellucian recommends that you disable all the fittings and start testing one by one.

    By disabling the fittings, the pipeline keeps its form and data. When the test button is used, it will not use the disabled fittings. Enabling the fittings one after another and running a test allows you to identify the fitting that is causing issues.

  • Always stringify before writing a CSV file:

    Whenever the pipeline requires output into a CSV file, you need to stringify the JSON response first. There are extra properties in the File Writer fitting, such as Add Newline and Generate Presigned URL, that provide benefits.

    Setting Generate Presigned Url to ON is especially useful if you want to verify the resulted file. The test will provide the URL in the payload so you can download the file.

  • Use JavaScript Transform to pre-process data:

    Sometimes it is necessary to create data structures or format the data that you want before processing it. Ellucian recommends using the Javascript Transform fitting for this action. It is the easiest way to add, edit, transform or recreate the structure and the data as needed. The example below shows a simple rename of the properties.

    function transform (message, context) {
  const data = message.payload;
  let newPayload = {};
  newPayload.firstName = data['First Name'];
  newPayload.middleName = data['Middle Name'];
  newPayload.lastName = data['Last Name'];
  newPayload.fullName = data['Full Name'];
  newPayload.gender = data['Gender'];
  newPayload.race = data['Race'];
  newPayload.ethnicity = data['Ethnicity'];

  newPayload.oldData = data;
  message.payload = newPayload;
  return message;
}

    It is also possible to collect data from the context and use it to modify the payload.

    function transform (message, context) {
  const data = message.payload;
  let newPayload = {};
  
  // The date of birth comes in a "month cardinalDay, year" format,
  // so we are going to transform it into a local String format.
  let dateStr = data['Date Of Birth'];
  newPayload.dateOfBirth = '';
  if(dateStr) {
    // An example of how to use context values defined as our pipeline parameters.
    let dateArr = dateStr.split(context.get('dateSeparator'));
    // Format the date to change from ordinal to cardinal number for the days.
    let newDate = dateArr[0].substring(0, dateArr[0].length - 2).concat(dateArr[1]);
    newPayload.dateOfBirthFormated = newDate;
    newPayload.dateOfBirth = new Date(newDate).toISOString();
  }
  
  newPayload.oldData = data;
  message.payload = newPayload;
  return message;
}

    It is also possible to collect data from the context and use it to modify the payload.

Common questions

Some common questions are answered.

During pipeline execution, after an error occurs, how can I find which fitting the error belongs to?

The Errors tab in Ethos Integration shows the fitting that caused the error. There is a View Errors link on the job run screen that takes you to an errors page. Or, you can manually search for the error on the Errors page by filtering on the Correlation ID, which is the same as the Job Run ID.

During the design phase, the TEST button reports the exact fittings that failed.

Why am I receiving a timeout error?

When testing, be advised that the pipeline may only execute for 60 seconds. Limit your data to a small number of records using filters or other parameters so that the pipeline can complete.

How do I successfully configure the SFTP Fitting by SFTP key?

Make sure you do the following:
  • Create a parameter, for example sftpKey of type string, with multiline enabled.
  • Copy the value of the key. It should include the comments as well. For example, -----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY----- ...etc.
  • If receiving file errors, make sure the path is correct. For example /home/fileName.txt or /fileName.txt instead of just fileName.txt.

When scheduling a job I can set the Hours. What time zone does it use?

You can enter the time in your local time zone and it will execute. Behind the scenes, time is stored as coordinated universal time (UTC).

Does the Data Connect job rerun again automatically if it fails due to any infrastructure or network issue?

There are various levels of retry or resiliency built in:

  • When you run a job, it goes to a queue. If the Data Connect back end is down, it waits there until it can be picked up.
  • Individual HTTP calls have retry logic (like retry 10x or so) and timeouts (wait about three minutes on an individual call). After all retries have failed, the overall job in the user interface would be marked as TIMED OUT and could be run again manually or automatically on the next scheduled interval.

How many job runs are retained for a job?

Data Connect retains the most recent 1000 job runs for a given job.

Filtering with JSON and Mustache

Data connect configuration fields use the Mustache library to evaluate expressions.

An example of the syntax use is using the Filter field to access a nested object in the Ethos Proxy Get with Filter fitting: "filter":"?criteria={\"vendorDetail\":{\"organization\":{\"id\":\"{{msg.payload.vendorOrganization.0.id}}\"}}}

In the above filter field, the expression msg.payload.vendorOrganization.0.id is accessing the first element of the vendorOrganization array, as Mustache uses dot notation to access elements. If a user attempted to use a JSON path such as {{vendorOrganization[0].id}}, it would be inaccurate as this is not a Mustache expression, therefore the expression vendorOrganization[0].id would be incorrect, and Mustache would interpret it as empty.

See https://mustache.github.io/ for Mustache documentation.

Whitelist the Data Connect IP addresses

Most network traffic from Data Connect to on-premise systems is through Ethos Integration.

In some instances, traffic does not go through Ethos Integration:
  • If you use an integration that involves SFTP access from Data Connect to your SFTP server. SFTP traffic does not go through Ethos Integration.
  • If you use the HTTP Fitting to call a custom API that is hosted on-premise only, not through Ethos Integration.

In these cases, your firewall rules should allow for inbound requests from the static IPs listed here.

Sources

These fittings consume data.

Ethos Consume Event fitting

The Ethos Consume Event fitting is used to consume events (change notifications or business events) from Ethos Integration.

After processing an event, use the Ethos Consume Confirm fitting to mark it as processed.

Change notifications

Change notifications are resource-based messages that give the current state of a resource at the time a change occurred. You receive change notifications when you subscribe to changes for a specific resource that an authoritative application owns.

A change notification does not contain information about what specifically changed in the source system (before and after values). It tells you what happened to the resource (operation) and what data the resource contains (content) at the time of the change.

Business events

Business events are event-based messages that show specifically what changed in a source system as a result of some event, such as an update to a person's name, in comparison to change notifications that only inform you about the operations and current data. Business events are not tied to resources that are exposed through an API, like change notifications are.

To create and subscribe to business events, see Create an event definition manually from the BEP user interface, Define business event notifications for extended data elements, and Subscribe to business events.

Considerations

The Ethos Consume Event and Ethos Consume Confirm fittings should be used together in the following order:
  1. Ethos Consume Event
  2. Fitting segments to perform necessary processing
  3. Ethos Consume Confirm

Pay attention to the following when using this fitting:

  • This fitting will request Ethos to return events using the last processed ID previously recorded by the Ethos Consume Confirm fitting. If no last processed ID has been recorded, this fitting will use a last processed ID of 0.
  • By default, multiple events are consumed in a batch. Configure the batch size using the limit configuration below.
  • It is the responsibility of the processing segments to preserve the event id so that it can be used in the Consume Confirm fitting. If the event id is not preserved (due to error, or intentional skip logic), then the last processed ID persisted by the Consume Confirm fitting is not updated.
  • If the behavior of your processing logic is such that a certain last processed ID does not reach the Consume Confirm fitting (due to error or otherwise), the last processed ID is not incremented. If a subsequent event is successfully processed, confirmation of that event implicitly confirms the prior event, because events are ordered.
  • Events will be pushed down the pipeline one at a time. Because of the streaming nature of an integration pipeline, the first event that was pushed down the pipeline may still be making its way through the later processing steps when the second event begins making its way through the first set of processing steps. Order of processing is maintained, but there is no transactional guarantee that the first event will be completely processed before the second event begins processing.
  • The Ethos Consume Event fitting can be used to either consume events (change notifications or business events) that trigger a job, or be used in a scheduled job that checks events. This is determined when you create a pipeline job, and select Schedule or Triggered by event in the Job Run Details. See Create a pipeline job.

Expected input

Optional message payload that is a JavaScript object.

Reference configuration

Configuration Description
Detail Required. Array of Ethos resources: A list of resources is available in the API Catalog.

Select to consume change notifications or business events.

Select Change notifications to consume change notifications from Ethos Integration. Specify the resource name and version. Select + Change Notification to add additional resources.

Note: Resource and version settings act as filters within the fitting. Events that do not match the configured resource/version are dropped and do not move forward in the pipeline. Because the subscriber queue is ordered (FIFO), events must still be confirmed to advance the queue. If no event reaches the Ethos Consume Confirm fitting, the job will retry repeatedly.

Select Business events to consume business events from Ethos Integration. All Business events associated with the subscribing application, based on the provided API key, will be consumed.
Limit Optional. Maximum number of messages to consume. Note: Ethos Integration defaults to 20 if not set, and has a top limit of 1000.
Target Optional. Dot-notation target within payload to put Ethos response. When not set it replaces the whole message payload.
Ignore Errors Optional. Flag that when set to true, it disables error reporting to Ethos when an error is caught. Use this in conjunction with errorPath to implement custom error handling further in the pipeline.
Error Path Optional. Dot-notation error path. Setting this will push original message forward with error details. Error path can specify a location in header or payload. When no location is specified it defaults to payload, in other words: error is the same as payload.error.
API Key

Optional. Name of a pipeline parameter which will contain the API key to be used by this fitting. When not specified ethosApiKey will be used.

If you have multiple Ethos Consume Event fittings, they must contain the same parameter name in the API Key field when using the Triggered by event option in the Job Run Details. See Create a pipeline job.

Expected configuration

{
  "class": "ethosConsumeChangeNotifications", // Name persits with Change Notifications for backwards compatibility.
  "config": {
    "resources": [ /* List of resources */ ], // Ethos resources - Required if consuming Change Notifications
    "businessEvents": "boolean", // Business Events Flag - Required if consuming Business Events
    "target": "string", // Optional - Dot-notation target within payload to put Ethos response. When  not set it replaces the whole message payload.
    "limit": "integer", //Optional, Maximum number of messages to consume. Note: Ethos Integration defaults to 20 if not set, and has a top limit of 1000. 
    "apiKey": "string", // Optional - Name of a pipeline parameter which will contain the the API key to be used by this fitting. When not specified `ethosApiKey` will be used. 
    "errorPath": "string", // Optional - Dot-notation error path. Setting this will push original message forward with error details. Error path can specify a location in header or payload. When no location is specified it defaults to payload, in other words: "error" is the same as "payload.error"
    "ignoreErrors": "boolean" // Optional flag that when set to true, it disables error reporting to Ethos when an error is caught. Use this in conjunction with errorPath to implement custom error handling further in the pipeline.
  }
}

Example fitting configuration for change notifications: 

"consumePersons": {
  "class": "ethosConsumeChangeNotifications",
  "config": {
    "resources": [{"name" :"persons", "supportedVersions":["7", "8.1"]}],
    "target": "changeNotification.result",
    "errorPath": "error"
  }
}

Example fitting configuration for business events: 

"consumePersons": {
  "class": "ethosConsumeChangeNotifications",
  "config": {
    "businessEvents": true,
    "target": "businessEvents.result",
    "errorPath": "error"
  }
}

Output

This fitting will push a new message for each event (change notification or business event) received in the response.

Optional message payload that is a JavaScript object.

Reference configuration

Configuration Description
Query Optional. When not provided, query string should be passed as incoming message payload
Target Optional. Dot-notation target within payload to put Ethos response. Only used if the incoming message payload is an object. When not set it replaces the whole message payload.
Ignore Errors Optional. Flag that when set to true, it disables error reporting to Ethos when an error is caught. Use this in conjunction with errorPath to implement custom error handling further in the pipeline.
Error Path Optional. Dot-notation error path. Setting this will push original message forward with error details. Error path can specify a location in header or payload. When no location is specified it defaults to payload, in other words: "error" is the same as "payload.error".

Example

The following is an example of how to use Ethos GraphQL.

  1. In order for this fitting to work, an Ethos Api Key should be created as a parameter. Click over the dropdown menu aside the pipeline name, select Edit Pipeline Settings, and add a new pipeline parameter named ethosApiKey. The name is reserved so it will always pick that parameter unless a different option is selected as the Api Key in the configuration.

Ethos Proxy Auth fitting

Use this fitting to obtain an Ethos authorization token.

All other Ethos fittings obtain authorization tokens automatically. However, if for some reason you need to obtain a token on your own, you can use this fitting.

Expected input

Message payload that is a JavaScript object.

Reference configuration

Configuration Description
Error Path Optional. Dot-notation error path. Setting this will push original message forward with error details. Error path can specify a location in header or payload. When no location is specified it defaults to payload, in other words: "error" is the same as "payload.error"
Api Key Optional. Name of a pipeline parameter which will contain the the API key to be used by this fitting. When not specified ethosApiKey will be used.
