Decrypt Data fitting

The Decrypt Data fitting supports PGP decryption with signature verification for data integrity and authenticity. It decrypts incoming encrypted data and returns the original data as string (or binary, if specified).

Note: The Decrypt Data fitting is currently a beta release for customers testing new functionality.

Expected input

Input to the fitting must be in a single payload.

The Decrypt Data fitting supports multiple input types.

Type Description
String Encrypted data in ASCII armored format.
Buffer/Uint8Array Encrypted data in binary format.
Array of strings Reducer fitting output of multiple encrypted text payloads.
Array of Buffers/Uint8Arrays Reducer fitting output of multiple encrypted binary payloads.

The fitting can process data from the entire message payload or extract from a specific path using JSONPath expressions.

Reference configuration

Configuration Description
Source Optional. String. JSONPath to locate data to decrypt in payload. Defaults to entire payload.
Private Key Required. String. The name of a pipeline parameter containing the PGP private key to use for decryption.
Passphrase Optional. String. The name of a pipeline parameter containing the passphrase for the private key, if the key is password-protected.
Verification Boolean. Optional. If true, verifies the data signature using the provided signer's public key. Decryption will fail if verification is unsuccessful.

Public Key. Required if verification is true. Pipeline parameter name containing the PGP public key to use for verification. String.
Target Optional. String. Dot-notation path to assign the decrypted output in payload. When not set it replaces the whole message payload.
Binary Optional. Boolean. If true, the output will be in binary format. If false, the output will be in text format.
Ignore Errors Optional. Boolean. If true, continues processing even on error.
Error Path Required if Ignore Errors is true. String. Dot-notation path for placing error info in the message.

Size limits

Maximum data size is 10MB.

Output

Text format (default): Decrypted data returned as a string when binary: false.

Binary format: Decrypted data returned as Buffer when binary: true.

Usage examples

Example fitting configuration for basic decryption:

{
  "class": "decryptData",
  "config": {
    "privateKey": "recipientPrivateKey",
    "passphrase": "keyPassphrase"
  }
}

Example specified paths and signature verification:

{
  "class": "decryptData",
  "config": {
    "privateKey": "recipientPrivateKey",
    "passphrase": "keyPassphrase",
    "source": "$.encryptedData",
    "target": "payload.decryptedData",
    "verification": true,
    "publicKey": "signerPublicKey"
  }
}

Example binary output and error handling:

{
  "class": "decryptData",
  "config": {
    "privateKey": "recipientPrivateKey",
    "passphrase": "keyPassphrase",
    "binary": true,
    "ignoreErrors": true,
    "errorPath": "payload.decryptionErrors"
  }
}
Delimited Formatter fitting

Use this fitting to format an object stream into a delimited report.

Expected input

The formatter expects each stream message payload to be an object. Payloads that are not of type object will be ignored by the fitting with no pass-through.

Reference configuration

The first three fields in the form: Fitting Name, Fitting Description, and Fitting Execution Condition are common to all fittings.

Main configuration

Configuration Description
Normalize Columns Optional. Column normalization is the process in which the formatter analyzes how many columns the report header row, detail rows, and report footer row contains and normalizes all of them by adding fillers. By default no normalization is done; rows will contain the configured amount of columns. To enable normalization the normalizeColumns must be explicitly set to true.
Header Optional. Header rows are content rows that can aid in the final report presentation or format. A header row is the very first row to be displayed. Example, a header row could contain the report title.
Detail Required. At least one detail column is required. The detail'configuration defines how each message payload is handled and laid out for each detail row.
Footer Optional. Footer rows are optional content rows that can aid in the final report presentation or format. The footer row is the last one to be displayed. Example, a footer row can contain totals.

Header

Configuration Description
Blank Header Value Optional. Empty row will be added as header.
Type Optional. Defines how the column should be interpreted. When not specified all columns are interpreted as literal. Columns of type eval are evaluated using a JavaScript interpreter. Values like simple mathematical expressions can be defined and be effectively rendered in the final report, Example. '{ "type": "eval", "value": "15 * 2" }' displays as: 30. Literal values are usually rendered as is and have little to no use for transformation functions unless they contain reference tags. Reference tags are Mustache type placeholders that are replaced at runtime.
Value Required if header is specified. column value to be rendered.
Transformation Functions Optional. Series of transformation functions applied to the queried source value. When more than one function is specified the series is executed in the order in which they are listed. The source value will always be automatically sent as a parameter to the functions.

Detail

Configuration Description
Column Headers Optional. Column headers are not included by default as part of the report detail. To enable them columnHeaders needs to be explicitly set to true.
Columns Required. The columns configuration property accepts a lists that can contain string values or configuration object for more advanced definitions. Both types can be found in a single list at the same time. When columnHeaders is enabled sometimes property names don't make for good column headers. The column object definition allows for a property path to be set along with a label.
Path Required. The path property allows for simple and nested object references. A simple string value represents location or path within the message payload object where the column value is located. If the columnHeaders property is set to true, the very same value will be used as column header. For flat objects, just the name of the property will suffice. For complex objects with nested objects, the string can handle dot notation.
Label Optional. The label for the column.
Accumulators Accumulators are defined buckets to analyze incoming data. These accumulators can be used by means of interpolation. Interpolation can be achieved by using Mustache type placeholders, which are replaced at runtime. For example, {{context.runId}} : Returns the pipeline's runId within the pipeline context. Additional details on Accumulators are available below.
Name Required. Name must be specified if an accumulator is added to detail. Each accumulator can be flexibly named, it can be based on reporting logic needs or some meaningful label.
Cumulative Function Optional. Each accumulator definition consists of a cumulative function name, and the parameters it needs. All cumulative functions expect numeric inputs. However, when a string is specified it is used as a mapping path to reference a message payload field.
Redaction Rules Optional. Redaction rules allows for the configuration of one or more columns to be blanked out or masked.
Match Optional, but at least this or type needs to be specified if the match property is included. By default columns to be redacted are matched with the detail column's path or label in a non case sensitive way. However, you can refine the matching algorithm by setting up type and case sensitive flags. Case sensitive specifies if the columns will be compared by taking into type casing. By default no case sensitivity (false) is used when comparing.
Type Optional, however this or case sensitive must be specified if match is added. Specifies which column field will be used to find which columns to redact. When not specified, both is assumed.
Column Optional. The columns configuration property accepts a lists or string values containing defined column paths or labels. It can also contain a string with reference tag to use context defined parameters, like: {{context.redactedColumns}}. It will be assumed that the referenced parameter is an array, otherwise the redaction rules will be ignored.
Mask When a mask is specified, instead of just blanking out a column value, it will be replaced with the mask's content.

Footer

Configuration Description
Blank footer value Empty row will be added as footer.
Type Optional. Defines how the column should be interpreted. When not specified all columns are interpreted as literal. Columns of type eval are evaluated using a JavaScript interpreter. Values like simple mathematical expressions can be defined and be effectively rendered in the final report, Example. { "type": "eval", "value": "15 * 2" } Displays as: 30. Literal values are usually rendered as is and have little to no use for transformation functions unless they contain reference tags. Reference tags are Mustache type placeholders that are replaced at runtime.
Value Required if footer is specified. Column value to be rendered.
Transformation Functions Optional. Series of transformation functions applied to the queried source value. When more than one function is specified the series is executed in the order in which they are listed. The source value will always be automatically sent as a parameter to the functions.

Transformation Functions

There are several transformation categories each of which contain one or more functions that can be used to change a mapped field's format or content.

  • string
    • toUpper : Converts all the alphabetic characters in a string to uppercase.
    • toLower : Converts all the alphabetic characters in a string to lowercase.
    • trim : Removes the leading and trailing white space and line terminator characters from a string.
    • truncate : Truncates a string if it exceeds a specified maximum length. Accepts one numeric parameter.
    • trimTruncate : Removes the leading and trailing white spaces and truncates a string if it exceeds the specified maximum length. Accepts one numeric parameter.
    • append : Appends one or more values to the input and returns the result.
    • prepend : Prepends one or more values to the input and returns the result.
    • substr : Gets a substring beginning at the specified location and having the specified length.
    • replace : Replaces text within input using a regular expression or search string.
    • split : Split a string into substrings using the specified separator and return them as an array.
    • toNumber : Converts a string value into a number.
  • number

    toFixed : Returns a string representing a number in fixed-point notation. Accepts one numeric parameter.

  • date

    format : Converts a date from an input format to the output format. Accepts two parameters, an input and an output date format strings. Based on momentjs format tokens.

  • array
    • unique : Returns a duplicate free version of list. Only works for primitive data types like strings and numbers, and is case sensitive. Aliases: removeDuplicates
    • without : Return an array version without provided values.
    • join : Adds all the elements of an array separated by the specified separator string. Accepts an optional delimiter parameter. If omitted, comma (,) is used to join array values.
    • find : Returns the value of the first element in the array where criteria or pathExpression predicate is true. For example,. preferred as criteria, and $.preference as pathExpression.
  • object
    • get : Returns the value of the first element matching pathExpression.
    • query : Returns an array of elements that satisfy the provided JSONPath expression, or an empty array if none were matched.
  • util
    • crosswalk : Translates the values in a single string or array based on crosswalk. Accepts one string parameter to specify which crosswalk configuration or function to use.
    • coalesce : Returns specified alternate value when input is undefined or null.
    • log : Outputs input content to console.log and passes-through its value. Used primarily for debugging purposes.
Example using the util.crosswalk function

Crosswalks are a way to customize the translation of one value to another. This is especially useful when data need to match a very specific set of enumerated values. When using util.crosswalk, you can reference tenant wide crosswalks or segment defined ones. The name of the crosswalk needs to be set as the first function parameter. If the crosswalk is not found the function will not be executed and ignored.

There are some built-in crosswalk functions that can be used out of the box with util.crosswalk:

  • iso3166.country.alpha3ToAlpha2 : Converts an ISO 3166-1 Country Code from Alpha-3 to Alpha-2.
  • iso3166.country.alpha2ToAlpha3 : Converts an ISO 3166-1 Country Code from Alpha-2 to Alpha-3.
  • hashmap.getValue : Returns the value of a given hashmap key. Uses the transformation input as key and requires a hashmap to be sent as input.

Accumulators

Accumulators are defined within the detail.accumulators configuration property. They are defined buckets to analyze incoming data and can be configured as custom properties to accumulate values to be used in the footer row.

Note: They are not available for header row use.*

Accumulator naming is flexible, it can based on reporting logic needs or some meaningful label. Each accumulator definition consists of a cumulative function name and the parameters it needs. For example:

  • Name: averageGrade
  • Cumulative Function: Average
  • Parameters: column1

Assuming there is an accumulator of name averageGrade defined, to include it as part of the Footer row you would configure it as:

  • Type: Literal
  • Value: {{accumulators.averageGrade}}

If the averageGrade calculation renders a number with a long decimal section, like 66.66666667. By using the number.toFixed Transformation Function you can standardize the way the value is presented across different scenarios.

  • Category: number
  • Function: toFixed
  • Enter Parameters: 2 (Click + button after entering the parameter)

This way you can transform any averageGrade value into a rounded 2 decimal position number. The example value of 66.66666667 would be transformed to 66.67.

Lastly, if you need to add an offset of 10 to that average. You would need to change the column type to eval and convert the value into a mathematical operation where accumulators.averageGrade gets added 10. Like this: {{accumulators.averageGrade}} + 10

In this case your value of 66.66666667 would be integrated into the mathematical expression and evaluated to 76.66666667, then transformed to 76.67.

Cumulative Functions

There are currently four implemented cumulative functions:

  • add: Adds the specified parameter value to the accumulator.
  • min: Keeps the accumulator updated with the smaller of a series of values.
  • max: Keeps the accumulator updated with the greater of a series of values.
  • avg: Keeps the accumulator updated with the cumulative average of a series of values.

All cumulative functions expect numeric inputs, however, a specific column name (as string) can be defined to make it the basis of value series to be analyzed.

Consider the following accumulators setup:

  • Accumulator01:
    • Name: counter
    • Cumulative Function: Addition
    • Parameters: 1
  • Accumulator02:
    • Name: col1Sum
    • Cumulative Function: Addition
    • Parameters: column1
  • Accumulator03:
    • Name: col1Average
    • Cumulative Function: Average
    • Parameters: column1

There are three defined accumulators: counter, col1Sum, and col1Average.

Their naming is totally flexible, but after they are set, their case-sensitive name must be used when using their reference tag on the footer row:

  • {{accumulators.counter}}
  • {{accumulators.col1Sum}}
  • {{accumulators.col1Average}}

For a series of payload:

// Payload 1
{ "column1": 100 }
// Payload 2
{ "column1": 50 }
// Payload 3
{ "column1": 50 }

The final cumulative values for each accumulator is:

  • counter : 3
  • col1Sum : 200
  • col2Average : 66.6666667
Examples

Provides examples of delimited formatter fitting.

Quick start

The only required configuration field is detail.columns. The rest of the fields are optional that are either ignored or defaulted.

The input will be a series of payloads:

[
  { "column1": "foo1", "column2": "bar1", "column3": "baz1" },
  { "column1": "foo2", "column2": "bar2", "column3": "baz2" },
  { "column1": "foo3", "column2": "bar3", "column3": "baz3" }
]

Delimited Formatter detail.columns configuration will be as follows:

  • Column01:

    Path: column1

  • Column02:

    Path: column2

  • Column03:

    Path: column3

Based on the configured mapping:

  • Each payload object field with key column1, column2, and column3 will be formatted into a comma delimited row.
  • Comma is the default record delimiter.

The result will be as follows

[
  "foo1,bar1,baz1",
  "foo2,bar2,baz2",
  "foo3,bar3,baz3"
]

Delimiter

The delimiting character, when not specified, will be defaulted to comma (,). When specified, it must be a one character string. The formatter will automatically wrap in double quotes any column value that contains the delimiting character, using the previous example and | as delimiter.

A payload with value:

{ "column1": "foo1", "column2": "bar1", "column3": "baz1" }

Will be formatted as:

[
  "foo1|bar1|baz1"
]

Normalize columns

Column normalization is the process in which the formatter analyzes how many columns the report header row, detail rows, and report footer row contains and normalizes all of them by adding fillers.

By default no normalization is done; rows will contain the configured amount of columns. To enable normalization the normalizeColumns must be explicitly set to true.

Configuration:

  • Header01:
    • Type: Literal
    • Value: header1
  • Header02:
    • Type: Literal
    • Value: header2
  • Column01:

    Path: column1

  • Column02:

    Path: column2

  • Column03:

    Path: column3

  • Column04:

    Path: column4

A sample report with no normalization:

[
  "header1,header2",
  "foo1,bar1,baz1,"
]

Now the same report with Normalize Columns ON:

[
  "header1,header2,,",
  "foo1,bar1,baz1,"
]

Extra commas were added at the end of header and footer rows to match the amount of columns in the detail section.

Header and footer rows

Not to be confused with detail column headers, header and footer rows are optional content rows that can aid in the final report presentation or format. A header row is the very first row to be displayed, while the footer row is the last one.

For example, a header row can contain the report title while the footer row can contain totals.

REPORT TITLE
column1,column2,column3
foo1,bar1,100
foo2,bar2,100
foo3,bar3,50
TIS THE LAST ROW

Header and footer configuration properties are lists that accept string (literal) values or configuration object for more advanced definitions. Both types can be found in a single list at the same time.

Each header and footer column is interpreted and then rendered. The logic follows this strict order:

  1. Reference Tag are replaced.
  2. JavaScript expressions are evaluated.
  3. Final value is rendered.

    More on Reference tags below.

To get a report just like the previous example, the fitting configuration must look like the following:

  • Header01:
    • Type: Literal
    • Value: REPORT TITLE
  • Column01:

    Path: column1

  • Column02:

    Path: column2

  • Column03:

    Path: column3

  • Footer01:
    • Type: Literal
    • Value: TIS THE LAST ROW

Even though the detail.columnHeaders is set to true, it has nothing to do with the report header and footer configurations.

Object Definitions

When a simple string is not enough to meet a header or footer column requirement, a configuration structure can be used to define it.

  • type: Optionally defines how the column should be interpreted: eval or literal. When not specified all columns are interpreted as literal.
  • value: Column value to be rendered.
  • transform: Optional list of transformation functions.

Transformation functions are documented in detail above. All but crosswalk transformations are supported by the delimitedFormatter.

Eval Columns

Columns of type eval are evaluated using a JavaScript interpreter. Values like simple mathematical expressions can be defined and be effectively rendered in the final report.

Consider the following examples:

  • Type: Eval
  • Value: 15 * 2

Displays as 30.

Date eval column:

  • Type: Eval
  • Value: new Date(2020, 0, 1)
  • Transformation Functions -> Category: date
  • Transformation Functions -> Function: format
  • Transformation Functions -> Enter Parameters: YYYY-MM-DD (Click + button after entering the parameter)

Displays as 2020-01-01.

Literal Columns

By default, when no type is specified, columns are interpreted as literal values. In essence, a configuration object of type literal with no transformations can be defined with just a string.

For instance, a column defined as just "foo", is syntactic sugar for:

  • Type: Literal
  • Value: foo

Literal values are usually rendered as is and have little to no use for transformation functions unless they contain reference tags.

Reference Tags

Reference tags are mustache type placeholders that are replaced at runtime.

It is the first step to be executed in the column interpretation logic. Any value coming out of the reference tag will be available for JavaScript expression evaluations and transformations, if they apply.

Reference tag data comes from two different sources: context and accumulators. When a tag is specified but cannot be mapped to a context or accumulator field, then it is replaced with empty string.

Context

Each pipeline has a context object that is shared across all fittings or segments. Context fields are available for use in header and footer rows.

Assuming the pipeline context contains field tenantId with value ellucian, to include it as part of header row you would configure it as:

  • Type: Literal
  • Value: {{context.tenantId}}

Accumulators

Accumulators are defined within the detail.accumulators configuration property. They are custom properties that accumulate values to be used in the footer row. **Note:**They are not available for header row use.

To learn more about Accumulators, and how to set them, check the accumulators section.

Detail rows

The detail configuration defines how each message payload is handled and laid out on each detail row.

String Definition

A simple string value represents location or path within the message payload object where the column value is located. If the columnHeaders property is set to true, the very same value will be used as column header.

For flat objects, just the name of the property will suffice. For complex objects with nested objects, the string can handle dot notation.

For a payload:

{
  "column1": "foo",
  "column2": "bar"
}

The columns definition would be:

  • Column01:

    Path: column1

  • Column02:

    Path: column2

In contrast, the following payload:

{
  "column1": "foo",
  "column2": {
    "id": 1,
    "name": "bar"
  }
}

To achieve the same results as the flat object payload, the columns definition needs to be:

  • Column01:

    Path: column1

  • Column02:

    Path: column2.name

Not all properties within a message payload need to be mapped to a report detail column. It all comes down to what really makes sense for the report. In the previous example column2.id was ignored.

Object Definition

When columnHeaders is enabled sometimes property names don't make for good column headers. The column object definition allows for a property path to be set along with a label.

The path property still allows for simple and nested object references.

For a detail configuration:

  • Column01:
    • Path: column1
    • Label: First Column
  • Column02:
    • Path: column2
    • Label: Second Column

A payload of:

{
  "column1": "foo",
  "column2": "bar"
}

Would render:

First Column,Second Column
foo,bar

Accumulators

Accumulators are fitting defined buckets to analyze incoming data. These accumulators can be later used within the report's footer row. Further details on accumulators can be found in the Accumulators section.

Redaction rules

The columns configuration property accepts one or more values containing defined column paths or labels. Interpolation is supported exclusively when setting columns as a single string value. Interpolation reference tags will use context defined parameters, like: {{context.redactedColumns}}. The product of the interpolation should render one or more values that will define de column paths or labels to be redacted, otherwise the redaction rules will be ignored.

Mask

When a mask is specified, instead of just blanking out a column value, it will be replaced with the mask content. The mask can be used in two different ways:

  • If only one character is specified then the character is used to replace all original value characters with the masking one.
  • If a word is specified, the word will be used instead of the original value.
// With a mask of '*'
'test' is masked with '****'

// With a mask of '<hidden>'
'test' is masked with '<hidden>'

Match

By default columns to be redacted are matched with the detail column's path or label in a non case sensitive way. However, you can refine the matching algorithm by setting up match.type and match.caseSensitive. Both settings are optional, but at least one of them needs to be specified if the match property is included.

  • type : Specifies which column field will be used to find which columns to redact. Possible values: path, label, and both. When not specified, both is assumed.

  • caseSensitive : Specifies if the columns will be compared by taking into type casing. Possible values: true or false. By default no case sensitivity (false) is used when comparing.

Output

Describes the delimited formatter fitting output.

This fitting pushes a new message with the same header as the incoming message.

When the incoming payload is of type object or array, the new message payload is the mapped outcome. Otherwise, message payload is passed through.

Delimited Parser fitting

Use the delimited parser fitting to parse a comma or tab delimited string into a JSON object.

Expected input

A message with a payload property containing a line of tab or comma delimited data. If the fitting has not received any prior lines, it will assume the first line it receives is the header line which guides how to structure subsequent lines received.

Reference configuration

Configuration Description
Target Optional property in the payload where the output should be placed. Otherwise, the payload will be the output array.
Dynamic Typing Optional property that allows numeric and boolean data to be converted to their types instead of string representations.
Header Optional list of header names to be used. This is useful when incoming delimited data does not have a header row.
Header Delimiter Optional delimiter to be used when building a header row from the configured header. Defaults to comma (,) when not specified.
Literal Quotes Optional. When enabled, double quotes are treated as normal text characters instead of quoted field delimiters. Use this option when your source data contains literal quotes that should not trigger CSV-style quoted field parsing. The default is Off.

Be aware that when the headers configuration field is set, even if the incoming data has a header row, the ones in the configuration will be used. The fitting will interpret the incoming header as data to be pushed forward. Furthermore, the headerDelimiter needs to match that of the incoming data, otherwise you can get unexpected parsing results.

When the Literal Quotes option is disabled, the fitting follows standard CSV-quoted field behavior. Fields enclosed in double quotes can contain delimiter characters without being split.

When the Literal Quotes option is enabled, double quotes are treated as plain text characters and delimiters inside of quoted text are treated as normal delimiters.

Output

A message with a payload containing a JavaScript object. Each object pushed by the fitting will have the same keys, which are the values from the header line.

Encrypt Data fitting

The Encrypt Data fitting supports PGP encryption with digital signing for data integrity and authenticity. It encrypts incoming data and returns encrypted data as binary (or ASCII armored, if specified).

Note: The Encrypt Data fitting is currently a beta release for customers testing new functionality.

Expected input

Input to the fitting must be in a single payload.

The Encrypt Data fitting supports multiple input types.

Type Description
String Text data to be encrypted.
Buffer/Uint8Array Binary data to be encrypted.
Array of strings Reducer fitting output of multiple text payloads.
Array of Buffers/Uint8Arrays Reducer fitting output of multiple binary payloads.

Reference configuration

Configuration Description
Source Optional. String. JSONPath expression to extract data from the message payload for encryption. Defaults to entire payload.
Public Key Required. String. Pipeline parameter name containing the PGP public key to use for encryption.
Signature Optional. Boolean. If true, the data will be digitally signed using the sender's provided private key.

Private Key. Required (String) if Signature is true. Pipeline parameter name containing the PGP private key to use for signing.

Passphrase. Optional. String. Pipeline parameter name containing the passphrase for the Private Key (if password-protected).
Target Optional. String. Dot-notation path to assign the encrypted output in the message payload. Defaults to replacing the entire payload.
Binary Optional. Boolean. If true, returns binary encrypted data. If false, returns ASCII-armored format.
Ignore Errors Optional. Boolean. If true, continues processing on error and routes to errorPath.
Error Path Required if Ignore Errors is true. String. Dot-notation path for placing error info in the message.

Size limits

Maximum data size for fitting input is 10MB.

Output

Binary format (default): Encrypted data returned as Buffer when binary: true.

ASCII armored: Encrypted data returned as ASCII armored when binary: false.

-----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-----
[encrypted content]
-----END PGP MESSAGE-----

Usage examples

Example fitting configuration for basic encryption:

{
  "class": "encryptData",
  "config": {
    "publicKey": "recipientPublicKey"
  }
}

Example of extracting data from a specific path and outputting as binary to pass down to fittings such as SFTP Put, File Writer:

{
  "class": "encryptData",
  "config": {
    "publicKey": "recipientPublicKey",
    "source": "$.sensitiveData",
    "target": "payload.encryptedData",
    "binary": true
  }
}

Example of how to sign a file using a passphrase and private key, and continue pipeline processing even if an error occurs:

{
  "class": "encryptData",
  "config": {
    "publicKey": "recipientPublicKey",
    "signature": true,
    "signingKey": {
      "privateKey": "signerPrivateKey",
      "passphrase": "keyPassphrase"
    },
    "ignoreErrors": true,
    "errorPath": "payload.encryptionErrors"
  }
}
Encrypt Data fitting example

This example provides sample pipelines demonstrating how to use the Encrypt Data fitting in Data Connect to apply Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) encryption to sensitive data before transferring it to external systems.

The Encrypt Data fitting enables secure, standards-compliant encryption of data within your pipelines. It supports (PGP) encryption with optional digital signatures, making it ideal for protecting sensitive information during data transfers to external partners, government agencies, or third-party systems.

In this example, the pipeline extracts student worker records from Banner, formats the data as CSV, encrypts it using the Encrypt Data fitting with PGP, and uploads the encrypted file to an SFTP server.

For example, a Human Resources manager that has student worker data that is stored in Banner. As an HR admin, you want to make sure that the data is encrypted every time you extract it from Banner, so that it can be safely transmitted for various purposes. Then a pipeline developer who is part of the security team wants to make sure that they are doing that encryption safely before transmitting that information.

The person who receives that encrypted student worker data would use a different pipeline with the Decrypt Data fitting.

Prerequisites

You will need the following before you begin:
  • Experience Premium with Integration Designer
  • Insights with the Extensibility license (for the Extract Data fitting)
  • PGP key pair for encryption and signing (public key, private key, and passphrase)
  • SFTP server credentials (private key, username, host, and destination path)

PGP encryption

The Encrypt Data fitting provides PGP encryption capabilities with the following features:

Type Description
PGP Encryption Encrypts data using a PGP public key, ensuring only the intended recipient can decrypt it.
Digital Signatures Optionally signs the encrypted data with a private key to verify authenticity and integrity.
Binary Output Produces binary encrypted output suitable for file transfer.
Error Handling Configurable error handling with the Ignore Errors option.

Included pipelines

encrypt-student-worker-data-mock

This pipeline uses mock data to demonstrate the Encrypt Data fitting without requiring a real connection.

For detailed steps, see Example: Extract a list and encrypt and upload to SFTP (mock test).

encrypt-student-worker-data

This pipeline extracts real student worker data from Banner, encrypts it using the Encrypt Data fitting, and uploads it to SFTP.

For detailed steps, see Example: Extract a list and encrypt and upload to SFTP.

Parameters

Parameter Description
publicKeyEncrypt The PGP public key used to encrypt the data file.
privateKeyEncrypt The PGP private key used to sign the encrypted file for authenticity verification.
passphraseEncrypt The passphrase associated with the PGP private key used for signing.
privateKeySFTP The private key used for authenticating with the SFTP server.
sftpUsername The username for authenticating with the SFTP server.
sftpHost The hostname or IP address of the SFTP server.
sftpFilePath The full file path on the SFTP server where the encrypted file will be uploaded.

Execution instructions

Security considerations

The Encrypt Data fitting provides multiple layers of security:
  • PGP Encryption: Uses asymmetric encryption where data is encrypted with a public key and can only be decrypted with the corresponding private key held by the recipient.
  • Digital Signatures: When signature: true, the fitting signs the data with your private key, allowing recipients to verify the data's authenticity and that it hasn't been tampered with.
  • Sensitive Parameters: All encryption keys and credentials should be marked as sensitive: true in parameters to ensure they are stored securely and not logged.
  • Secure Transfer: Combined with SFTP, provides end-to-end security for data in transit.

Other Use Cases for Encrypt Data Fitting

The Encrypt Data fitting is essential for scenarios requiring secure data transfer:
  1. Payroll exports to external payroll providers
  2. Financial data transfers to auditing firms
  3. HR data synchronization with third-party HR systems
  4. Student records exports for verification services
  5. Vendor data exchanges requiring encryption compliance

File Output

The pipeline generates a PGP-encrypted .gpg file containing the student worker data in CSV format. The file is uploaded to the specified SFTP location with the configured filename.

Example: Extract a list and encrypt and upload to SFTP (mock test)

Create a pipeline that demonstrates the encryption and SFTP upload workflow using mock student worker data.

About this task

This pipeline is designed for testing and development purposes without requiring a database connection.
This test version of the pipeline:
  • Generates synthetic student worker data using a JavaScript Transform fitting
  • Demonstrates the full Encrypt Data fitting workflow with mock data
  • Is useful for testing encryption configuration without affecting real data

Procedure

  1. In Ellucian Experience, click the Integration Designer card.
  2. Select or create a package:
    1. Select the Integration package where this new pipeline will be created.
    2. If needed, create a new package.
    3. In the Packages area, click +.
    4. Enter a unique name for the package.
    5. Optional: Add a description.
    6. Click Save.
    7. Select the new package from the list to continue.
  3. Create a new pipeline:
    1. In the Pipelines area, click + PIPELINE.
    2. Enter a unique name for the pipeline (for example, Encrypt Student Worker Data Pipeline Mock).
    3. Optional: Add a description. For example, This pipeline demonstrates the encryption and SFTP upload workflow using mock student worker data. It is designed for testing and development purposes without requiring a database connection.
    4. Click Save.
    5. Click the pipeline name to open it.
    6. To set up parameters, near the pipeline name, click the drop-down menu and select Edit Pipeline Settings.
    7. Add the following new pipeline parameters:
      1. publicKeyEncrypt
        • Label: PGP Public Key
        • Description: The PGP public key used to encrypt the student worker data file.
        • Type: String
        • Required: True
        • Sensitive: True
        • Multiline: True
        • Persistent: True
      2. privateKeyEncrypt
        • Label: PGP Private Key for Signing
        • Description: The PGP private key used to sign the encrypted file for authenticity verification.
        • Type: String
        • Required: True
        • Sensitive: True
        • Multiline: True
        • Persistent: True
      3. passphraseEncrypt
        • Label: PGP Passphrase
        • Description: The passphrase associated with the PGP private key used for signing.
        • Type: String
        • Required: True
        • Sensitive: True
        • Persistent: True
      4. privateKeySFTP
        • Label: SFTP Private Key
        • Description: The private key used for authenticating with the SFTP server.
        • Type: String
        • Required: True
        • Sensitive: True
        • Multiline: True
        • Persistent: True
      5. sftpUsername
        • Label: SFTP Username
        • Description: The username for authenticating with the SFTP server.
        • Type: String
        • Required: True
      6. sftpHost
        • Label: SFTP Host
        • Description: The hostname or IP address of the SFTP server.
        • Type: String
        • Required: True
      7. sftpFilePath
        • Label: SFTP Destination File Path
        • Description: The full file path on the SFTP server where the encrypted file will be uploaded.
        • Type: String
        • Required: True
    8. Click Save.
  4. To build the first segment for this example, configure the JavaScript Transform fitting:
    1. from the Transformations menu, click JavaScript Transform.
    2. Enter Generate Mock Student Worker Data as the fitting name.
    3. Optional: Enter a description. For example, Generates mock student worker data for testing the encryption and SFTP upload workflow without requiring a database connection.
    4. Set Push Undefined to True.
    5. Set Stop On Error to False.
    6. Enter the following: 
      "function transform(message, context) {
  message.payload.studentWorkers = [
